title: Targeting Price And Financial Stability In Ghana: The Role Of Monetary Policy And Macroprudential Regulations
snippet: Examining the effect of Ghana's macroprudential regulations and monetary policy on the nation's financial and price stability is the main objective of this study. It specifically looks at how these policies interact and what effect they have on Ghana's prices and financial stability. This is done using the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to evaluate quarterly data from 2013 Q1 to 2022 Q1 provided by the Bank of Ghana (BoG), Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), and World Development Indicators (WDIs). The results show that macro-level prudential regulations have no long-term association with financial stability, but they have a favourable and significant short-term effect. Furthermore, the existence of monetary policy boosts the short-term effects of macro-level prudential regulations on financial stability but has no significant long-term influence. Additionally, without macro-level prudential regulations, monetary policy has a detrimental, albeit slight, effect on price stability; nevertheless, in their presence, the study finds a notable and statistically significant positive effect in the long-run. The study proposes as a recommendation that Ghana maintain its framework for managing inflation, using measures to control liquidity, borrowing costs, inflationary pressures, and foster stability, including policy rates and macro-level prudential regulations, particularly the primary reserve requirement ratio. Immediate concerns about financial stability can be addressed using a coordinated approach that combines macroprudential regulations and monetary policy, while fine-tuned macro-level prudential regulations should be the principal tool for long-term stability preservation.

title: The Effect of Article 78 (1) of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana on the Oversight Role of the Parliament of Ghana
snippet: The Study was undertaken to identify how the Parliament of Ghana performs its oversight role in relation to Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana; to determine whether Article 78(1) affects the oversight role of the Parliament of Ghana; and to contribute to public debate on whether Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution should be amended. To address the objectives of the Study, The 1992 Constitution of Ghana, The Standing Orders of the Parliament of Ghana, books on how the Parliament of Ghana functions, the internet and other sources of existing literature on parliamentary oversight role and executive-parliament relations were consulted. Further, questionnaires were administered to one hundred and twenty (120) Members of the House to collect primary data on the subject matter. Interview guides were also used to tap the experiences of seven (7) key informants including three (3) veteran Parliamentary Staff. The Study indicated that the Parliament of Ghana performs its oversight role by using its Committee System to undertake investigations and scrutiny of policies; asking Ministers Questions; and moving Motions. Furthermore, the Study revealed that Article 78(1) which places an injunction on the President to appoint majority of Ministers from the Parliament of Ghana, undermines the oversight role of the Parliament of Ghana. This is evidenced by the fact that 54.2% of those to whom questionnaires were administered and six (6) out of the seven (7) key informants interviewed thought Article 78(1) affects the oversight role of the Parliament of Ghana more adversely than favourably. The conclusion of the Study was that, Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Ghana should be amended to have strict separation of powers in order to strengthen the Parliament of Ghana to perform its oversight role more effectively.

title: An examination of the role played by Ghana’s legislature in the management of the COVID-19 pandemic
snippet: In the wake of the recently emerged COVID-19 pandemic, legislatures were regarded as one of the important government institutions that can help cushion nations against the economic and social disruptions inflicted by the health crises, given the important roles they play in policymaking within political systems. This paper examines the roles played by Ghana's legislative institution in the management of the COVID-19 pandemic. The paper further explores some of the challenges to legislative activities during the height of the pandemic. From a content analysis of a variety of literature drawn from Parliamentary Proceedings, online journal articles, official documents, and news from credible media outlets, we found that Ghana's legislative institution was crucial to the country's management of the pandemic as they played important roles such as passing COVID-19 related laws, financial oversight, and providing a check on Executive actions. The main challenge to Parliamentary activities was the demand for rapid legislation, which weakened Parliamentary oversight and scrutiny functions. The study makes some recommendations to strengthen legislative responses to future pandemics.

snippet: Tafenoquine is a promising new 8-aminoquinoline drug that may be useful for malaria prophylaxis in non-pregnant persons with normal glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) function. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled chemoprophylaxis trial was conducted with adult residents of northern Ghana to determine the minimum effective weekly dose of tafenoquine for the prevention of infection by Plasmodium falciparum. The primary end point was a positive malaria blood smear result during the 13 weeks of study drug coverage. Relative to the placebo, all 4 tafenoquine dosages demonstrated significant protection against P. falciparum infection: for 25 mg/week, protective efficacy was 32% (95% confidence interval [CI], 20%-43%); for 50 mg/week, 84% (95% CI, 75%-91%); for 100 mg/week, 87% (95% CI, 78%-93%); and for 200 mg/week, 86% (95% CI, 76%-92%). The mefloquine dosage of 250 mg/week also demonstrated significant protection against P. falciparum infection (protective efficacy, 86%; 95% CI, 72%-93%). There was little difference between study groups in the adverse events reported, and there was no evidence of a relationship between tafenoquine dosage and reports of physical complaints or the occurrence of abnormal laboratory parameters. Tafenoquine dosages of 50, 100, and 200 mg/week were safe, well tolerated, and effective against P. falciparum infection in this study population.

title: Development of a HACCP Plan for a Model Cold Pressed Virgin Coconut Oil Industry in Ghana
snippet: The positive health effect of virgin coconut oil has emerged stronger among Ghanaians, but its safety is less considered with regard to processing in commercial quantities in Ghana. The objective of this study was to develop a HACCP plan for cold pressed virgin coconut oil (VCO) processors in Ghana.  The study considered the manufacturing line of GKV Investments limited as a model to implement a HACCP plan. The effectiveness of the HACCP plan was based on achieving a wholesome and safer cold pressed VCO which is free from food safety risk and capable of meeting laid down requirements.  Two Critical Control Points (CCPs) were identified in the HACCP implementation: CCP1 was at incoming raw material (fresh mature coconut) reception. CCP2 was at tubular centrifugation process step. Finished product testing was outsourced from accredited laboratories traceable to Ghana Standards Authority and Aspirata testing laboratory in South Africa to allow adequate verification and validation of adopted control measures. Both reports yielded positive results: Pesticide residues and heavy metals (lead and Arsenic) were not detected in the product. Moisture content was 0.07%, Free Fatty Acid (FFA) was 0.2 mgKOH/g (0.02%), and Peroxide value was 8.27%. Microbiology criteria of the finished product were all met:  E.coli, Salmonella, and Coliforms were not detected in the product, Aerobic Plate Count was < 1.0 x 100   cfu/g, and Yeasts/Moulds count was   < 1.0 x 101 cfu/g. The fatty acid composition of saturated fats (MCFA) was within specification with lauric acid recording 50.1% (50125.90 mg/100g). This indicates that the HACCP plan was effective at producing safer and quality cold pressed virgin coconut oil.

title: Evaluation of request forms submitted to the haematology laboratory in a Ghanaian tertiary hospital
snippet: Background: Laboratory request forms provide information about the laboratory test being requested for. They carry demographic data and other information such as location of patient, laboratory number, doctor’s name, signature of the doctor, telephone number of the requesting doctor. Omission of information on the forms may lead to laboratory errors. The aim of this study was to evaluate the level of completion of laboratory request forms at the haematology department of a Ghanaian tertiary hospital. Methods: Three thousand request forms submitted to the haematology department between January and April 2010 were retrieved and studied. The information provided on each request form was recorded in a spread sheet and analyzed. Results: The patient’s age and sex were missing in 25.6% and 32.7% of the forms respectively. About half of the request forms did not have the patient’s location. No clinical detail was provided on 22.7% of the forms. Doctors were more likely to sign their request forms and provide a name but they all failed to provide an address or a contact telephone number. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that, the standard of completion of request forms was poor. Essential information required on the forms was often missing. This can lead to limited advice given by laboratory physicians and may increase the potential for errors. Conversely, provision of all the information needed on the forms will aid laboratory diagnosis and enhance patient care and save time and resources. There should be closer interaction between clinicians and laboratory personnel to improve quality of services.

title: Impact of malaria diagnostic refresher training programme on competencies and skills in malaria diagnosis among medical laboratory professionals: evidence from Ghana 2015–2019
snippet:
Background: The quality of malaria test results is crucial for optimal patient treatment and care. The Ghana Health Service is successfully shifting from presumptive clinical diagnosis and treatment of malaria to the Test, Treat and Track (T3) initiative. In line with the initiative, the National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) set out to improve the capacity of medical laboratory professionals in Ghana through a ﬁve-day Malaria Diagnostic Refresher Training (MDRT) to build competencies and skills in malaria diagnosis, especially in the three components of microscopy: parasite detection, species identiﬁcation and parasite quantiﬁcation. This study evaluates the impact of the training on malaria microscopy.
Methods: The training which was based on the World Health Organization basic malaria microscopy training guide employed presentations and practical approaches to malaria diagnosis. A total number of 765 medical laboratory professionals from various health facilities across the country were trained every other year from 2015 to 2019 and were included in this evaluation. Evaluation of this training was done using pre-test and post-test microscopy scores.
The Negative Binomial ﬁxed eﬀect model was used in determining the overall eﬀect of the training in improving the competencies of the participants on malaria microscopy.
Results: The ability of the medical laboratory professionals to correctly detect malaria parasites increased signiﬁ- cantly from a median score of 64% prior to the training to 87% after the training (p < 0.001). The competencies of the medical laboratory scientists to correctly identify malaria parasite species and quantify the number of malaria parasites increased signiﬁcantly from a median score of 17% and 20% pre-test to 78% and 50% post-test, respectively (p < 0.001). The results showed that participants’ competency level and skill to perform malaria microscopy (species identiﬁcation, parasite quantiﬁcation and detection of malaria parasites) increased by approximately two folds after the training compared to the no-training scenario (adjusted rate ratio = 2.07, 95% CI 2.01–2.13, p < 0.001).
Conclusion: The MDRT programme signiﬁcantly improved participants’ performance of malaria microscopy over a short period of time.

title: Prevalence and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Pattern of Neisseria gonorrhoeae in Kumasi, Ghana
snippet:
Background: In most African countries, including Ghana, treatment of the Neisseria gonorrhoeae
infection is based on syndromic management owing to lack of laboratory equipment and resources
in primary care facilities where most patients first visit.
Aim: The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and evaluate
its susceptibility pattern to standard antimicrobials used for empirical treatment of the infection in
patients that attended Ellolab Diagnostic Centre at Kumasi from November 2014 to July 2017.
Methodology: Four hundred and twenty-seven (427) clinical specimens from suspected patients
were cultured on chocolate agar. Positive cultures were tested for resistance against twelve antimicrobial agents using the disk diffusion method.
Results: N. gonorrhoeae was identified in 117 of the clinical samples. This represents an overall
prevalence of 27.4%, with 39.3% and 60.7% occurring in males and females respectively. Maximum
cases were observed in the 16-24 age group. Interestingly, the organism showed high levels of
resistance to the nationally recommended drugs for first-line empirical treatment; Ceftriaxone 85.5%,
Ciprofloxacin 46.2% and Amikacin 1.7%.
Conclusion: The local susceptibility trends of N. gonorrhoeae need to be monitored closely in order
to establish appropriate local empirical therapy.

title: Impact assessment of the national rooftop solar programme  (NRSP) on residential homes-A case study of beneficiaries in Accra-Ghana
snippet:
Worldwide attention has been drawn towards renewable energy especially in the
sphere of solar energy in a bid to tackle global energy deficit and environmental crises
such as global warming, air and water pollution. Solar energy offers an encouraging
solution to this search as it is a less polluting renewable energy resource and can be
easily converted into electricity through the use of Photovoltaic (PV) systems. Solar
PV systems provide electric energy by absorbing and converting sunlight into
electricity. It achieves this by an arrangement of several components known as the
Balance of System (BoS) and solar panels. PV systems range from small, rooftop
mounted or building integrated systems with capacities from a few to several tens of
kilowatts (kW), to large utility scale power stations of hundreds of megawatts. In
2007, Ghana was faced with drastic energy crisis and this lasted till the year 2016,
though it is not permanently solved in the country. There were persistent, regular and
unpredictable electric power outages. This satirically birthed the term “Dumsor”
literally meaning “off-on” to represent the worsening power crisis the country was
plagued with. In a bid for the government to solve this challenge, the Government of
Ghana (GoG), under the auspices of the Energy Commission of Ghana (EC) began an
implementation of a Capital Subsidy Scheme where free rooftop solar panels up to a
maximum capacity of 500 Watts peak to residential beneficiaries. This study therefore
sought to assess the impact of the rooftop PV solar systems on beneficiaries in Accra
since its implementation and to forecast its expected benefits or otherwise in the long
term for Ghana. Results showed from the study revealed that, there was very low
patronage of the programme by the citizenry. Only about 0.10% (2,449/2,270,000) of
the total population of the people in Accra applied to benefit from the project. There
was a further reduced number of beneficiaries (727) who actually got the solariii
systems to be installed in their homes. The mean expenditure on power and
consumption levels of beneficiaries before and after installation of the rooftop solar
PV systems was significantly reduced. Results showed that every reduction in
consumption level was accompanied by almost two times reduction in cost of
electricity. However, the major challenge beneficiaries had faced with the rooftop
solar PV systems were the batteries. In effect, the project was a good programme and
should be continued.

title: Solar eclipse of March 29, 2006
snippet: A total solar eclipse occurred at the Moon’s ascending node of orbit on Wednesday, March 29, 2006, with a magnitude of 1.0515. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, thereby totally or partly obscuring the image of the Sun for a viewer on Earth. A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon's apparent diameter is larger than the Sun's, blocking all direct sunlight, turning day into darkness. Totality occurs in a narrow path across Earth's surface, with the partial solar eclipse visible over a surrounding region thousands of kilometres wide. Occurring about 1.1 days after perigee, the Moon's apparent diameter was larger.

title: Prevalence and Antimicrobial Susceptibility Pattern of Neisseria gonorrhoeae in Kumasi, Ghana
snippet:
Background: In most African countries, including Ghana, treatment of the Neisseria gonorrhoeae
infection is based on syndromic management owing to lack of laboratory equipment and resources
in primary care facilities where most patients first visit.
Aim: The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and evaluate
its susceptibility pattern to standard antimicrobials used for empirical treatment of the infection in
patients that attended Ellolab Diagnostic Centre at Kumasi from November 2014 to July 2017.
Methodology: Four hundred and twenty-seven (427) clinical specimens from suspected patients
were cultured on chocolate agar. Positive cultures were tested for resistance against twelve  antimicrobial agents using the disk diffusion method.
Results: N. gonorrhoeae was identified in 117 of the clinical samples. This represents an overall
prevalence of 27.4%, with 39.3% and 60.7% occurring in males and females respectively. Maximum
cases were observed in the 16-24 age group. Interestingly, the organism showed high levels of
resistance to the nationally recommended drugs for first-line empirical treatment; Ceftriaxone 85.5%,
Ciprofloxacin 46.2% and Amikacin 1.7%.
Conclusion: The local susceptibility trends of N. gonorrhoeae need to be monitored closely in order
to establish appropriate local empirical therapy.

title: Haematological and biochemical reference values for healthy adults in the middle belt of Ghana
snippet: Background: Reference values are very important in clinical management of patients, screening participants for enrolment into clinical trials and for monitoring the onset of adverse events during these trials. The aim of this was to establish gender specific haematological and biochemical reference values for healthy adults in the central part of Ghana. Methods: A total of 691 adults between 18 and 59 years resident in the Kintampo North Municipality and South District in the central part of Ghana were randomly selected using the Kintampo Health and Demographic Surveillance System and enrolled in this cross-sectional survey. Out of these, 625 adults made up of 316 males and 309 females were assessed by a clinician to be healthy. Median values and nonparametric 95% reference values for 16 haematology and 22 biochemistry parameters were determined for this population based on the Clinical Laboratory and Standards Institute guidelines. Values established in this study were compared with the Caucasian values being used currently by our laboratory as reference values and also with data from other African and western countries. Results: Reference values established include: haemoglobin 113–164 g/L for males and 88–144 g/L for females; total white blood cell count 3.4–9.26109/L; platelet count 88–3526109/L for males and 89–4036109/L for females; alanine aminotransferase 8–54 U/L for males and 6–51 U/L for females; creatinine 56–119 mmol/L for males and 53–106 mmol/L for females. Using the haematological reference values based on the package inserts would have screened out up to 53% of potential trial participants and up to 25% of the population using the biochemical parameters. Conclusion: We have established a panel of locally relevant reference parameters for commonly used haematological and biochemical tests. his is important as it will help in the interpretation of laboratory results both for clinical management of patients and safety monitoring during a trial

title: Wilberforce donates stationery to NDC
snippet: A native of Enyan Denkyira in the Central Region, Wilberforce Andrews has donated office stationery to the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC) Headquarters in Accra. The items, which included A4 sheets, Bic pens, office pins and flat files, he said, were meant to support the party ahead of its upcoming internal elections. Briefing the media, […]
content: A native of Enyan Denkyira in the Central Region, Wilberforce Andrews has donated office stationery to the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC) Headquarters in Accra. The items, which included A4 sheets, Bic pens, office pins and flat files, he said, were meant to support the party ahead of its upcoming internal elections. Briefing the media, he said his donation formed part of his continuous support for the party since he joined ahead of the 2024 general elections. "I am here today because I believe in supporting the structures that keep our democracy working. Even the smallest tools matter when it comes to running a smooth and peaceful election," he said. "As a son of Enyan Denkyira, I have been contributing to national development. This donation is a continuation of that commitment," he added. Wilberforce Andrews wanted to contest the last general elections as an independent presidential candidate. He, however, abandoned his ambition to join the NDC, which was the then largest opposition party and campaigned vigorously for the party. This decision, he explained, was borne out of the fact that the campaign message of President John Dramani Mahama who was the flag bearer of the party, aligned with his vision. The items which were donated on Wednesday, 14th October 2026, were received by the Director of Administration of the NDC, Emmanuel S. Zumakpeh. In a letter of acknowledgement, Director Zumakpeh stated, "This thoughtful contribution will greatly support the administrative work of the party and we are grateful for your consistent kind gesture and commitment to our collective cause." He assured that the donated items would be put to effective use in advancing the work of the party. Mr Andrews said as a good citizen of Ghana, he has been participating in the development of the country and felt it necessary to support the party's preparations for the elections. "I want to encourage other well-meaning Ghanaians to also support in their own small way. Nation building is not the job of government alone," he said. title: Feature: Balancing Or Diluting Electoral Commission
snippet: “Except as provided in this Constitution or in any other law not inconsistent with this Constitution, in the performance of its functions, the Electoral Commission shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority” – Article 46 of the Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992. Until 1968, this country did not […]
content: “Except as provided in this Constitution or in any other law not inconsistent with this Constitution, in the performance of its functions, the Electoral Commission shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority” – Article 46 of the Constitution of the Republic of Ghana, 1992. Until 1968, this country did not have an Electoral Commission. The work, done by the Electoral Commission, was done by the Ministry of Local Government, and their task was to ensure the conduct of free, fair and honest elections. Do not remind those of us septuagenarians how elections were conducted in the 40’s, 50’s and (early) 60’s. You (if you are a septuagenarian) may remember the 1964 Referendum held on 31st January 1964. It was to amend the 1960 Constitution to turn the country into a one-party state. Total number of voters was 2,776,372 (100%). There were ‘0’ (0.00%) invalid or blank votes. Those who said “Yes” were 2,773,920 (99.91%). Those who said “No” were 2,452 (0.09%). The Workers (Builders) Brigade were all over the place supervising the voting, and who dare you show your face as opposition to the Convention People’s Party! The results of the Referendum were announced, and the whole Ghana became a one-party state, that is, CPP became the sole legal party. Dr. Kwame Nkrumah became President for life (for the country and the party). Nkrumah had the power and authority to dismiss the Supreme and High Court judges at will. We were very young then, but we saw everything “fili-fili”. The “No” boxes were sealed, and one person in CPP could vote many times. With the military coup in 1966, the Siriboe Committee was formed by the National Liberation Council (NLC) to re-examine the electoral procedures and make recommendations to restructure local governance. Justice Johnson Boateng Siriboe’s 16-member Committee, overwhelmed by incidences of political manipulation and rigging, recommended the creation of a permanent independent body – the Interim Electoral Commission of 1968, paving the way for the present-day Electoral Commission. Justice V. C. R. A. C. Crabbe, who became the Electoral Commissioner, resigned in 1971 to go back to the Bench, leaving G. A. K. Bonsu to be the next Commissioner. Under Kutu Acheampong’s National Redemption Council, Isaac Abban was appointed Interim Electoral Commissioner in 1972. Abban went into hiding after the 1978 referendum on Union Government (Unigov). Joseph Kingsley Nyinah took over and he supervised the general election which brought Dr. Hilla Limann to power in the Third Republic, after J. J Rawlings handed over the AFRC in 1979 to civilian rule. The present Electoral Commission is established by the Electoral Commission Act (Act 451) of 1993, and the first Chairman of the Fourth Republic was Kwadwo Afari-Gyan (1993–2015). Afari-Gyan was succeeded by Charlotte Osei, who was sacked by Nana Akufo-Addo on assuming the presidency in 2018, and replaced by Jean Adukwei Mensa. The persons in the Electoral Commission are supposed to be non-partisan. Hence, in the pre-2024 election, Mahama had to question President Akufo-Addo’s appointments to the Electoral Commission: “Ehu abo wɔnom, enti wonom de NPP foɔ complete akɔ Electoral Commission — the appointments of Rev. Ofori Boateng, Salima Appiahene… Yɛbɛyɛ wɔn te sɛ Azumah Nelson…” (They are now drenched in fear, hence they have assembled NPP people into the Electoral Commission, but we will deal with them just as Azumah Nelson did…). The Television Stations were active last Saturday, TV3 programme. So also was “Joy News” hosted by Lardi Anyenini. Excellent panel at both stations; excellent phone-ins. You could be sure Professor Agyemang-Duah would be available to supply the missing links and add his invaluable experienced opinion: “Can she (Emelia Agbenyo) on her own manipulate the electoral process? I don’t believe so… Raise the bar, don’t lower it… The Afro-Barometer findings should be our guide… we should try and retain the independence of the judiciary as well as that of the Electoral Commission… why this unnecessary brouhaha?… The President should be guided by history, having been President before… he should sanitise our democratic march… he should not take the wishes of the public for granted… the call by CODEO should be a guide”. With this accusation, the least one would expect President Mahama to do would be for him to appoint Emelia Affi Agbenyo, a known NDC activist, into the E. C. as a Deputy Commissioner to make a total of seven (7) as per the 1992 Constitution, Felix Ofosu Kwakye would “employ all his communication skills” to justify Emelia Agbenyo’s appointment. Did Ofosu Kwakye mean that NDC seeks by this appointment to “balance” the equation of the institution or the NDC seeks to “dilute” the effect of NPP’s packing of the E. C. with its members? Wouldn’t the explanation have been better as: “We (NDC) criticised Nana Akufo-Addo’s (NPP) appointments to the EC and we criticised same, we now see that he was right, so we want to do same.” But the question remains: “Can’t NDC get an equally suitable person for Madam Agbenyo’s job? Perhaps we have to believe Martin Kpebu’s claim that “President Mahama was not properly advised, instead of subjecting itself to all these unnecessary bashings? Ofosu Kwakye would say “NPP waged a war of attrition” (and the claim is championed by Hopeson Adorye). He adds “the closure of Radio…Gold was NPP’s “darkest hour” (as far as this march for democracy was concerned). Did we vote (in 2024) for “reset” or “equalization”? Certainly, we voted for the former (reset) and not the latter (equalisation). So, you will see that Jean Mensa was appointed by Akufo-Addo, but his man, Bawumia, could not win… Going back, Charlotte Osei was appointed by Mahama, but in 2016, Akufo-Addo beat Mahama to win the Presidency. We would repeat what Nana Annor Amihere II said in the Chronicle of Tuesday October 20, 2026 on “Are we Practicing Democracy or Kakistocracy?”… (1) A Two-Party State and the “Pull Him Down” Syndrome: Our Constitution provides for multi-party democracy. In practice, power passes between the NDC and the NPP. Each treats the other as an enemy to be destroyed, rather than a rival to be defeated at the polls. Under this arrangement every institution becomes a prize and every appointment becomes a weapon. The “pull-him-down” syndrome has moved beyond ordinary politics. It now poses a real danger to the stability of the state. (2) The Electoral Commission: A Referee in Party Colours: An election is only as credible as its referee. Both parties know this. Both have tested it. During its time in office, the NPP placed on the Commission persons the NDC described as party affiliates. The NDC protested loudly. Then-candidate John Mahama went further and proposed that Article 43(2) be amended so that Parliament must approve new Commissioners. In 2026, President Mahama swore in two new Deputy Chairpersons. One is a long-serving E. C. official. The other, Mrs. Emelia Affi Agbenyo, has been publicly described by the NPP as an open NDC campaign team member. At the swearing-in, the President said he expected no preferential treatment for himself, his party or his government. Those are good words. Yet the reform he championed in opposition has not come. title: “By 2030, Raw Minerals Should No Longer Leave Our Shores” — Prez Sets Bold Agenda for Africa’s Mineral Sovereignty
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has set an ambitious target for Ghana to end the export of unprocessed mineral ores by 2030, challenging African leaders to turn the continent’s vast mineral wealth into industries, jobs and lasting prosperity for its people. Addressing the Mining in Motion Summit on the theme “The Accra Reset and Africa’s Mineral […]
content: President John Dramani Mahama has set an ambitious target for Ghana to end the export of unprocessed mineral ores by 2030, challenging African leaders to turn the continent’s vast mineral wealth into industries, jobs and lasting prosperity for its people. Addressing the Mining in Motion Summit on the theme “The Accra Reset and Africa’s Mineral Sovereignty,” the President argued that Africa could no longer afford to supply the raw materials powering the world’s industries while importing finished products made from its own resources. “Will our copper bring electricity to African homes? Will our bauxite power African factories?” he asked, challenging delegates to rethink how mineral agreements are negotiated and how the benefits of extraction are shared. Drawing attention to Ghana’s long history of exporting raw minerals, President Mahama said the country had watched its manganese and bauxite leave through its ports for decades, only to import finished products manufactured elsewhere. That pattern, he argued, had cost Ghana valuable opportunities for skilled employment, technological advancement and industrial growth. The Accra Reset, he explained, was intended to change that relationship by strengthening domestic processing and connecting mineral extraction to manufacturing. He cited ongoing efforts in the bauxite-to-aluminium value chain, iron ore and steel production, manganese processing and gold refining as important steps towards retaining more value locally. The President also announced his intention to pursue a phased prohibition on exports of unprocessed mineral ores, backed by the necessary legal measures and clear implementation timelines. Pres Mahama said Africa’s mineral ambitions would be stronger if countries worked together rather than competed against one another for investment on unfavourable terms. He called for regional value chains that would allow minerals mined in one country to be processed in another and supplied to manufacturers across the continent. The President maintained that mineral development could not be considered successful if communities were left with polluted rivers, damaged farmland and few lasting benefits. Liberia’s Vice President, H.E Jeremiah Kpan Koung Sr. in his key note address, echoed the call for Africa to move beyond raw mineral exports and build a stronger industrial base around its natural resources. He said the continent needed a common policy direction that respected each country’s sovereignty while establishing shared principles for fair returns, environmental protection and competitive industries. He outlined priorities including reliable energy and transport infrastructure, stronger geological institutions, transparent resource management, meaningful community participation and support for responsible artisanal and small-scale mining. He also called for closer regional cooperation on technology transfer, local procurement and mineral processing, stressing that mining communities must continue to benefit long after extraction ends. The Vice President urged African countries to turn existing continental frameworks into practical projects with measurable results, supported by investment, financing and regular reviews of progress. His message reinforced the summit’s central challenge: Africa must use the growing global demand for minerals not simply to increase exports, but to build industries, expand opportunities and secure a greater share of the prosperity generated by its own resources. title: NPP must support recovery of state funds to improve workers’ salaries – Anaba
snippet: The Member of Parliament for Garu, Dr Thomas Anaba, has challenged the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Minority in Parliament to support efforts to recover public funds allegedly misappropriated under the previous administration, arguing that the money could help improve salaries for public sector workers. He said the Minority should support efforts to retrieve the funds […]
content: The Member of Parliament for Garu, Dr Thomas Anaba, has challenged the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Minority in Parliament to support efforts to recover public funds allegedly misappropriated under the previous administration, arguing that the money could help improve salaries for public sector workers. He said the Minority should support efforts to retrieve the funds rather than criticising the 9% salary increase negotiated for public sector workers for 2027. “What the minority should be concerned about now is to find those who squandered our monies, and we are searching for them. We want them to come back to the country and provide those monies so that government can pay workers better,” he said. Speaking on Eyewitness News on Friday, October 30, 2026, Dr Anaba questioned why the Minority was criticising the salary agreement instead of supporting efforts to hold individuals accused of misappropriating public funds accountable. “I have not seen the minority turn anywhere to support government and even call on judges to fast-track all those who have been alleged to have misappropriated government funds…” he said. “Why is it that they are not interested in us recovering the money so that we can pay the workers well, but they are interested in inciting workers against government?” Dr Anaba's comments come amid a dispute between the government and the Minority over the 9% salary increase agreed for public sector workers in 2027. The Minority has described the increment as inadequate, citing rising living costs and previous salary adjustments. The Garu MP accused the NPP of contributing to the country's economic difficulties through what he described as financial mismanagement during its administration. He also urged former administration officials facing allegations of financial wrongdoing to return to Ghana and answer questions about their stewardship of public funds.

title: Afenyo-Markin: NDC must accept the same scrutiny demanded under Akufo-Addo
snippet: Minority Leader, Alexander Afenyo-Markin has challenged the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) to accept the same level of scrutiny it demanded of the Nana Addo Akufo-Addo administration when it was in opposition. His comments come amid the Minority’s criticism of the government’s handling of the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa. The Minority has questioned […]
content: Minority Leader, Alexander Afenyo-Markin has challenged the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) to accept the same level of scrutiny it demanded of the Nana Addo Akufo-Addo administration when it was in opposition. His comments come amid the Minority’s criticism of the government’s handling of the evacuation of Ghanaians from South Africa. The Minority has questioned the GH¢49.72 million reportedly spent on evacuating 1,964 Ghanaians, citing alleged discrepancies in payment registers, duplicate entries and gaps in supporting documents. It has called for an independent audit of the exercise and demanded the resignation of Foreign Affairs Minister, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, threatening to pursue a vote of censure if he remains in office. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 30, the Effutu MP said the NDC could not champion accountability while in opposition and become uncomfortable with it after assuming power. He accused the governing party of applying double standards on accountability, arguing that it now treats criticism of government decisions as political hostility after spending eight years insisting that questioning those in power was essential to democracy. “The NDC spent eight years teaching Ghanaians that questioning government was patriotism. Today, the same people appear offended that Ghanaians have taken those lessons seriously,” he wrote. He questioned whether the standards of accountability had changed simply because a different political party was now in government. “Apparently, accountability was a democratic virtue when the NPP was in power, but it has suddenly become political persecution now that the NDC occupies the seat of government,” he said. Afenyo-Markin cited the NDC's record in opposition, saying the party scrutinised contracts, challenged appointments, interrogated public expenditure and questioned government promises under the previous administration. He insisted that similar scrutiny of the current government should not be regarded as an act of hostility. “Public office is not a personal possession; it is a public trust. Holding office does not grant anyone immunity from criticism. Questioning a contract is not a personal attack on the person who approved it. Demanding transparency is not an expression of hatred. Asking government to honour its promises is not an attempt to undermine it. It is simply democracy at work,” he said. The Minority Leader pledged that the opposition would continue scrutinising government contracts, public expenditure and policy commitments. “The Mighty Minority will continue to read the documents, examine the contracts, question public expenditure, and measure government promises against actual performance,” he said. He maintained that the NDC should be held to the same accountability standards it demanded of the NPP while in opposition. “The standard members of the NDC demanded when they were in opposition should be the same standard they must live by, and we, the Mighty Minority, will not renege,” he added.

title: Mahama Reveals Nuclear Power Talks With Russia
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has disclosed that Ghana has initiated discussions with Russia on establishing the country’s first nuclear power station, as part of efforts to secure reliable electricity for industrialisation. Speaking at the third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow on Thursday, October 29, the President said cooperation with Russia in nuclear energy could help Ghana […]
content: President John Dramani Mahama has disclosed that Ghana has initiated discussions with Russia on establishing the country’s first nuclear power station, as part of efforts to secure reliable electricity for industrialisation. Speaking at the third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow on Thursday, October 29, the President said cooperation with Russia in nuclear energy could help Ghana strengthen its electricity supply and support its long-term industrial development. “Industrialisation requires reliable and affordable electricity,” President Mahama told participants at the summit, stressing the importance of developing a diversified energy mix that includes renewable energy and the peaceful use of nuclear power. He said Ghana had maintained a longstanding relationship with Russia in nuclear science, dating back to 1964, when the Soviet Union provided the country with a nuclear reactor for scientific and research purposes. The President also recalled that several Ghanaian nuclear scientists had received training in Russia to operate the reactor, describing the historical cooperation as a foundation on which the two countries could build stronger energy partnerships. “We have initiated discussions with Russia on the establishment of Ghana's first nuclear power station,” he said. President Mahama identified energy security as a critical area for cooperation between Africa and Russia, noting that inadequate electricity supply remained a major obstacle to the continent's economic progress. He said Russia's experience in renewable and nuclear energy presented opportunities for partnerships that could help African countries address their energy challenges while supporting industrial growth. The President's remarks form part of Ghana's broader push to deepen economic and technological cooperation with Russia, moving beyond historical diplomatic relations towards practical partnerships that deliver tangible development outcomes. He urged both sides to translate the goodwill between them into concrete projects capable of improving people's lives, arguing that the success of the summit would ultimately be measured by the benefits communities derive from the agreements reached. “The most lasting expression of our friendship will be the progress that people can see in their communities and their lives,” he said. By Jesse Otoo

title: Nursery and tree management practices for Improved germination, seedling quality and fruit Characteristics of cape st. Paul wilt disease Tolerant coconut varieties
snippet:
To meet the increasing demand for Cape St. Paul Wilt Disease (CSPWD)
tolerant coconut seedlings, this research was carried out to develop
interventions for improving seed nut germination and vigour, seedling quality
and vigour and Sri Lanka Green Dwarf (SGD) fruit characteristics. Seven (7)
different experiments were carried out to assess pre-nursery practices, seedling
spacing and fertilizer application, ablation and fruit thinning towards addressing
deficiencies in coconut nursery and tree management practices. Fully burying
Sri Lanka Green Dwarf crossed Vanuatu Tall (SGD x VTI) coconut hybrid
seed nut in decomposed sawdust at pre-nursery stage improved germination
rate, speed of germination and germination index respectively by 33%, 30%
and 98% relative to the control. A treatment combination of 60-cm triangular
spacing and fertilizer application of 47.3:96.6:126.0:28.4 g seedling·1
N:P20S:K20:MgO produced good quality SGD x VTI coconut hybrid
seedlings with averagely 34% higher vigour, 12% bigger collar girth, 11 %
wider canopy diameter and 5% increase in height relative to the control.
Thinning ofSGD coconut variety to 10 fruits per bunch increased crude protein
and Vitamin C contents of fresh fruits by 31 % and 42% respectively; and
average fresh fruit weight by 32% and its components: husk, shell, kernel and
water averagely by 42%, 61 %, 42% and 65% respectively. Findings of prenursery
studies are recommended for dissemination to appropriate entities to
improve seed nut germination rate and increase supply ofSGD x VTI coconut
hybrid seedlings to fanners. Further research is recommended for assessing
field perfonnance of SGD x VTI coconut hybrid seedlings as affected by
potassium nitrate soaking treatment, planting depth or nut size.

title: Studies on Soil Amendment Strategies and Neem Products for the Management of Insect Pests of Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus (L.) Moench)
snippet:
The effect of different soil amendment strategies, and neem products for the management of
insect pests of okra was studied in the field at the Ashaiman irrigation project site.
The insect pests encountered fell into seven orders belonging to twenty-three families. The
important ones among these were Aphis gossypii (Glov.), Bemesia tabaci (Genn.), Dysdercus
spp. Podagrica uniformis (Jac.), Heliothis armigera (Hb.) synonym Helicoverpa armigera
(Hb,), Sylepta derogata (Fab.), Anthonomus grandis (Boh.) and Empoasca spp. Calidea spp.
Pachnoda spp and Riptortus were also found attacking okra fruits in Ashaiman. The
beneficial insects included Coccinella spp., Odonata spp. Cheilomenes vicinia (Muls.) and
Rhinocoris rapax (L.).
The neem products were less harmful to the beneficial insects and controlled homopteran
pests better than the synthetic insecticide, dimethoate. Dimethoate was less effective in
managing A. gossypii. and B. tabaci probably due to the development of resistance in these
insects.
In the field, the compost treatments improved plant vigour and enhanced their tolerance to
pest attack than the sole chemical fertilizer, and gave significantly higher response in all
yield indices studied. The sole fertilizer treated plants, however, performed better than the
untreated control in fruit yield, damage, and vegetative yield indices studied. The combined
effects of compost and aqueous neem seed extract (ANSE) at 50 g/1 enhanced okra
resistance to insect pests attack, and improved yield and marginal benefit of over 100% the
cost of production. ANSE was better than the formulated neem product, Neemazal at (2
ml/1), in managing the insect pests of okra, and compared favourably well with the synthetic
insecticide, dimethoate 40% EC (75 ml/151).
As a production package for okra, plants should be treated with compost prepared
from cocoa husk, rice straw and poultry manure at (500 g/plant), ANSE (50 g/1) sprayed
with cone nozzle is recommended.

title: Genetically modified food in Ghana
snippet: Genetically Modified (GM) food crops were introduced into Ghana in 2013 after the 2011 Biosafety Act 831 permitted their introduction. By 2014, “confined field trials” of GM rice and cowpea in the Ashanti region and cotton in the three northern regions of the country were underway.
