title: Nigeria Labour Congress Challenges Tinubu’s Fresh External Loan Request
snippet: The National President of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), Comrade Joe Ajaero, has criticised President Bola Tinubu’s request to the National Assembly to approve fresh borrowing for external loans worth $20.5 billion and €1.45 billion. While appearing on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, Ajaero stated that the basis for the loan was not clear […]
content: The National President of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC), Comrade Joe Ajaero, has criticised President Bola Tinubu’s request to the National Assembly to approve fresh borrowing for external loans worth $20.5 billion and €1.45 billion. While appearing on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief on Thursday, Ajaero stated that the basis for the loan was not clear to the Labour movement. “If you come out to tell us that the subsidy is gone, that you are making more money and then you are giving more money to states, what is the justification for continually borrowing from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and other agencies when there is enough money?” The Labour leader argued that the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, and other agencies lending money to the Nigerian government are doing the country a disservice. According to him, the debt profile is killing the country. He stated that all oil-producing states are now making more money due to the Middle East conflict. “If the 2026 budget was prepared with crude oil price benchmarked at $70 per barrel and now sells above $100 per barrel due to the US-Iran crisis, should this country still be collecting loans?”, Ajaero asked. Responding to the position of the Labour Congress, Ajaero said that NLC does not approve loans and does not even know when the money is paid into the pocket of the federal government. He urged every Nigerian and agencies to take responsibility for the matter and ask why the federal government is collecting another loan, adding that if the National Assembly rejects the loan, the Federal government will not get any loan. The latest request comes amid growing debate over the Tinubu administration’s borrowing plans and the country’s rising debt burden. In April, Channels Television reported that the Federal Government increased its planned borrowing for 2026 by ₦11.31 trillion to ₦29.20 trillion, while projecting a fiscal deficit of ₦31.46 trillion and debt-servicing costs of ₦15.81 trillion. The government has faced criticism over its continued reliance on loans despite the removal of the petrol subsidy, which was expected to free up resources for development. The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate Peter Obi warned in April that Nigeria was heading towards a debt crisis, arguing that the government had continued borrowing despite the subsidy removal. Credit: channelstv.com

title: Feature: Filthy Men In Sexual Rampage
snippet: Scrooge! A squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner… (Stave 1) A Christmas Carol (1843) – Charles Dickens OBUASI – a name that is simply translated as under the rock – has been famous in Ghana’s history for a long time because of its gold. We cannot discount the sweet oranges of the town: Obuasi […]
content: Scrooge! A squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner… (Stave 1) A Christmas Carol (1843) – Charles Dickens OBUASI – a name that is simply translated as under the rock – has been famous in Ghana’s history for a long time because of its gold. We cannot discount the sweet oranges of the town: Obuasi ankaa – wo)! And people from far and near enjoyed the juice, and the town attracted people from all over Ghana for its wealth: besides the local Adansis, we also have Fantes, Akuapims, Kwahus, Assins, Frafra, Grushies, Dagartis, Hausas, Ewes, Gas, Nzema,…. a lot of whom have made Obuasi their second-home. Before 1875, the indigenous people extracted gold from stream beds and shallow rock reefs. French explorer Marie Joseph Bonnat obtained the first mining rights in June, 1875. Joseph Ellis and Joseph Biney were two Fantes who put in a claim of land stretching 265 km square (the Ellis Mine). The Fante duo transferred their rights to Edwin Arthur Cade in August 1895. In 1897, the British incorporated the Ashanti Goldfields, naming the company as Obuasi Gold Mine which was once headed by our friend, Sir Sam Jonah as the Chief Executive Officer. As to be expected, Obuasi is home to many educational institutions: Obuasi Senior High Technical School, a co-educational second cycle public school; Christ the King Catholic Senior High School; St. Margaret Senior High School; the College of Integrated Health Care; and a campus of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. Akrokerri where we had our training as teachers lies about seven kilometers away, and we had our teaching practice in one Middle School in Obuasi town. (But for the Senior High, it was Vakpo Secondary School that we went to teach for the National Service almost fifty years ago). We were taught at Akrorkerri by our “Education” master that as teachers we were going to be “in loco parentis” (in the place of a parent). The child is entrusted to the care of the teacher who has the responsibility of not only teaching him, but also discharging the duties that would normally be exercised by the parents, including counselling the child: for this to be possible, there should exist “rapport” between the teacher and the pupils… but each person should know where the limits are, and educationists ought to know this. Comes in Zakaria Abdulai and that headmaster must have read “Tom Brown’s School Days” (the 1857 novel by Thomas Hughes) and may have imbibed the thinking: “Boys will be boys” (rough, noisy, impulsive) rather than “Boys will be men” (with emotional maturity, accountability and empathy) with a PhD (Dr) in Educational Administration, 25 years of experience in educational leadership and running Obuasi SHTS since 2015. How old is he? Is he married? He has allegedly abused that “contract”. The story as it unfolds, is bizarre and scandalous. It is all over the place – the whole of Ghana, the whole world – and now with the Internet… YouTube, Facebook, TikTok A headmaster – not a tutor – interdicted over allegations of having sexual relations involving close to 19 female students in the school, leading to forced abortions…! Students went on demonstration, and this led to the arrest and detention of a number of the students. Also arrested were two tutors – Messrs. Brefo and Appiah. The school was closed down, close to three months, for the violent demonstration… burning of the headmaster’s car. Police investigations led to the discovery of an object resembling a foetus buried in the school’s compound… who may have buried the foetus, and from whose body? Stinking. And, but for Manasseh Azure Awuni and Joy News, the truth would have been hidden from the public… – Zakaria would have enjoyed his position as NDC Secretary of Juaben Constituency; he could have won the Chairmanship… on and on to even Regional or National Chairmanship! Before we proceed let us condemn the topic given this story by the “Catholic Standard” of Sunday October 25, being “Schools of Shame”! Why and how this topic? We are Catholics and we never miss “The Catholic Standard” from 1974… The story was well captured: “Two campuses, more than a dozen girls, one nation asking: who is guarding our daughters? Ghana’s classrooms, meant to be sanctuaries, are under a cloud. Two senior high schools, one in the north and one in the heart of Ashanti, now stand at the centre of allegations that have shaken parents, shocked the Church and forced the government to act… Obuasi Senior High Technical School… two security men at Bolgatanga Girls Senior High School (BOGISS) are facing trial for defilement, Adams Nyaaba Idrisu, 72, and Elvis Adongo, 38… The Mental Health … chaired by the Executive Secretary Mr. Humphrey Matey Kofie, has demanded to know whether the BOGISS child is safe, supported and back in school… Until the courts and investigators have done their work, the presumption of innocence must stand. But the safety of every girl in Ghana’s schools must not wait on a court (?) verdict.” Excellent, But what makes the schools “Schools of Shame”? It is a shame that whereas Sir Sam Jonah and others like him carried out themselves and portrayed Obuasi to the world in great honour, people like the headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, have wrecked that stupendous recognition. Notable people have given very useful comments and observations; the panel on last week’s Saturday programme on TV 3 “The Big Issue” was marvellous; Martin Kpebu wishes there would be a stop to “white-washing” of the allegations, and that all implicated parties, including the committee that reported, teachers responsible for action against the miscreants must all be held responsible… Joy FM Newsfile as well captured it. You would also have appreciated Dr. Yaw Adutwum’s discussion at “Mpu-ne-Mpu” on UTV. The brilliant ex-MP explained the role of the Ghana Education Service and that of the Ministry of Education, explaining the “mandatory training” given at the beginning of every year to teachers that includes “sexual abuse” and “sexual harassment” as well as “mandatory reporting” (Not to the headmaster or the school authorities, but rather to a “third party” like DOVVSU). Let us warn teachers and all those who handle our kids. The days of yore are over. Gone are the days when women would panic when school vacations come and fear the female students would grab their husbands — call the female students “Koforidua flowers”. Gone are the days when teachers would go to some schools and engage in immorality, with female students and calling same “bush allowance”. The headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, has been interdicted by the Ghana Education Service, pending investigations by the Police and Court action. The Court will tell whether what he did can be an offence under the Criminal Offences Act, 1960 (Act 29 as amended by Act 554). Rape: Sections 97 and 99 of Act 29 classified as a first degree felony carrying a sentence ranging from a minimum of 5 years to a maximum of 25 years OR Defilement (Natural or unnatural carnal knowledge of a child under the age of 16 … (either male or female victims) classified as a felony without any justifiable defence of consent. Carrying a minimum sentence of 7 years and a maximum of 25 years. Check Section 99: “Whenever, upon the trial of any person for an offence punishable for this Code, it is necessary to prove carnal knowledge or unnatural knowledge, the carnal knowledge or unnatural carnal knowledge shall be deemed complete upon proof of the least degree of penetration.” There are reports that some of the school girls who had given statements to the Police are going to withdraw their statements. Whom does this surprise? Political maneuvering, societal lobbying, religious pressure, in the end, it becomes a wasted effort by all of us, and the alleged criminal will go home unscathed when we are told by the Police, “It is a foolish case”. Are the following institutions going to sit down and watch this case die: Ghana Police Service (CID, DOVVSU), Office of the Attorney-General, the Ghana Education Service, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Human Rights Committee of Parliament, Civil Society Organisations like the Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA)… For more news , join The Chronicle Newspaper channel on WhatsApp: https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VbBSs55E50UqNPvSOm2z

title: Ways To Keep Your Kidneys Healthy
snippet: What is a kidney? The kidneys are two fist-sized organs that filter your blood. Your kidneys are part of your urinary system. Your kidneys filter about 200 quarts of fluid every day — enough to fill a large bathtub. During this process, your kidneys remove waste, which leaves your body as urine (pee). Most people pee […]
content: What is a kidney? The kidneys are two fist-sized organs that filter your blood. Your kidneys are part of your urinary system . Your kidneys filter about 200 quarts of fluid every day — enough to fill a large bathtub. During this process, your kidneys remove waste, which leaves your body as urine (pee). Most people pee about 2 quarts daily. Your body reuses the other 198 quarts of fluid. Each kidney also helps balance your body’s fluids (mostly water) and electrolytes. Electrolytes are essential minerals that include sodium and potassium. Watch Your Salt This mineral affects people in different ways. For some, it seems to raise the amount of protein in their urine. That can harm your kidneys or make kidney disease worse if you already have it. Lots of salt also raises your chances of high blood pressure, a typical cause of kidney disease, and kidney stones, which can be very painful and possibly cause damage without treatment. Drink Enough Water Water helps get important nutrients to your kidneys and move waste to your bladder in the form of urine. If you don’t drink enough, the tiny filters inside your kidneys can get stopped up and lead to kidney stones and infections. Even mild dehydration can damage your kidneys if it happens often enough. Four to six cups a day is typically about right, but you might need more if you’re sick or out in the heat. Take Care With Antibiotics These bacteria -fighting drugs can damage your kidneys if you use them too often. It can happen even if you’re perfectly healthy, though it’s more serious if your kidneys don’t work as well as they should. Some are more likely to cause problems. Skip Herbal Supplements Supplement makers don’t have to prove their products are safe, and some can damage your kidneys. Those can be especially harmful if you have kidney disease because they can make the condition worse or affect how some medicines work. Talk with your doctor before trying any herbal supplement. Eat Healthy Your kidneys process everything you eat or drink, including anything that’s bad for you, like lots of fat, salt, and sugar. Over time, a bad diet can lead to high blood pressure, obesity, diabetes, and other conditions that are hard on your kidneys. A healthy diet has lots of vegetables , fruits, and whole grains, and few processed foods. Exercise Just like a healthy diet, this helps prevent conditions like diabetes and heart disease that can lead to kidney damage. But don’t try to go from couch potato to gym rat in a day. Too much exercise can also damage your kidneys if you’re not ready for it. Work your way up to 30 to 60 minutes at least five days a week. Start slow if you haven’t done it in a while, and check with your doctor first if you have health issues. Get Screened It’s important to know your risk for kidney disease. It’s more likely if you or close relatives have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, or a family history of kidney failure. In these cases, your doctor might suggest specific kidney tests as part of your regular checkup. The earlier you catch it, the easier it is to treat and sometimes even stop. Be Careful With Alcohol If you’re healthy, a drink or two isn’t likely to hurt your kidneys. But binge drinking (having more than four drinks in less than 2 hours) can cause sudden, serious damage and possibly lead to long-term problems. And alcohol often can dehydrate you, which can keep your kidneys from working well and lead to weight gain, liver disease, high blood pressure, and other conditions that put more stress on them. Quit Smoking Smoking raises your risk of kidney cancer and damages blood vessels, which affects your kidneys by slowing blood flow to them. Plus, smoking can affect certain drugs that treat high blood pressure. This is serious because uncontrolled high blood pressure is a leading cause of kidney disease. Manage Health Problems The two most common conditions that affect your kidneys are diabetes and high blood pressure. A balanced diet and regular exercise can help keep both under control. With diabetes, it’s also important to keep a close eye on your blood sugar and take insulin when you need it. For high blood pressure, check your numbers regularly and take all medicines exactly as your doctor prescribes them. Source: webmd

title: Feature: Religion Was Used To Conquer Africa -Food Is Next
snippet: Whoever controls our seed, our soil and our stomach will control our future. A warning to Ghanaians and Africans. Africa once lost its land while its people were being taught to pray. Today the threat has moved from the pulpit to the farm gate. Ghana now depends on imports for more than 95 per cent […]
content: Whoever controls our seed, our soil and our stomach will control our future. A warning to Ghanaians and Africans. Africa once lost its land while its people were being taught to pray. Today the threat has moved from the pulpit to the farm gate. Ghana now depends on imports for more than 95 per cent of its agricultural inputs, including fertiliser, pesticides and improved seed. In March 2026 the price of urea rose by more than half in a single month because of conflict in the Middle East. Government had to move from subsidised to free fertiliser to keep farmers planting. That is what dependence looks like. At the same time, our farmers are abandoning the slow, natural methods that fed our ancestors. Weedicide has replaced the cutlass. Chemical fertiliser has replaced the fallow. Purchased seed is replacing the seed our grandmothers kept above the hearth. Ghana has approved its first genetically modified crops and passed a seed law that critics say favours commercial breeders over farmers. Vultures, wild mushrooms and land snails are vanishing from our landscape. This article explains how we arrived here, separates the real dangers from the rumours, and sets out what Government, traditional authorities, farmers and families must do now. A nation that cannot feed itself from its own seed will one day take orders from whoever sells it food. The Bible and the Land A saying is often repeated across Africa. When the missionaries came, they had the Bible and we had the land. They told us to close our eyes and pray. When we opened them, we had the Bible and they had the land. Whatever one's faith, the lesson is about method. Conquest rarely announces itself. It arrives through something we trust and welcome. Faith was one such door. Trade was another. Today the door is the input shop: the bag of seed, the bottle of weedicide and the sack of fertiliser. Kwame Nkrumah warned in 1965 that the new form of control over Africa would be economic rather than military. He called it neo-colonialism. A country can hoist its own flag and still have its policies shaped by those who hold its purse. The same is true of its stomach. How Our Forefathers Farmed Our ancestors practised shifting cultivation, which agricultural scientists call bush fallow. A family cleared a plot, farmed it for two or three seasons, then moved on and allowed the forest to return. Leaf litter, ash, roots and soil life restored the fertility over several years. No bag of fertiliser was needed. Weeding was done with the cutlass and the hoe. It was hard work, and it kept people strong. Our grandparents walked to the farm, carried their harvest home and ate what they grew: cassava, plantain, cocoyam, yam, garden eggs, kontomire, palm nut soup and fish from our rivers and sea. Many of them remained active and clear-minded into very old age. Seed was a family inheritance. The best maize cobs were hung over the hearth. The best groundnuts were set aside before any were sold. Each community held its own varieties, suited to its own soil and rainfall. No company owned them and no one paid a royalty to plant them. What Has Changed on Our Farms Some of the change was unavoidable. Our population has grown many times over, so land can no longer rest for ten or fifteen years. Fallow periods have shrunk and soils are tired. Much of the change, however, is a matter of choice. Many young people no longer want to weed by hand. They want to plant today and harvest tomorrow. Weedicides such as glyphosate and paraquat are sprayed in place of the cutlass. Insecticides are applied without measurement, without protective clothing and often close to harvest. Empty chemical containers end up storing drinking water. Spray drift reaches the streams that villages drink from. As a safety and environmental professional, I see the consequences. Acute pesticide poisoning among farmers is under-reported. Residues are found on vegetables sold in our markets. Fish and soil organisms suffer in sprayed catchments. These are documented hazards, and they are preventable. Our health has changed too. Strokes, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and obesity now strike Ghanaians in their forties and fifties. Doctors attribute this to many causes acting together: refined and processed foods, sugar, less physical work, stress and tobacco. Careless chemical use on our food adds a risk we do not need. The common thread is our distance from the way our ancestors farmed, ate and worked. The Real Battleground Is Seed In June 2022 the National Biosafety Authority approved Ghana's first genetically modified crop, a pod borer-resistant Bt cowpea. In early 2024 it approved fourteen more genetically modified products, eight of maize and six of soybean, for food, feed and industrial use. A long legal challenge by civil society groups was later dismissed by the Human Rights Court. Fairness requires that we state the other side. The Bt cowpea was developed by Ghanaian scientists at CSIR-SARI. Its supporters say it needs far fewer insecticide sprays than ordinary beans, which would reduce chemical exposure. Regulators say every approval passed a safety review. The deeper question is ownership. In November 2020 Parliament passed the Plant Variety Protection Bill, modelled on an international convention known as UPOV 1991. The Peasant Farmers Association of Ghana, the General Agricultural Workers Union, the National Catholic Secretariat, the Ghana Muslim Mission and others objected. They warned that it restricts farmers from selling and exchanging seed of protected varieties and tilts the law towards large commercial breeders. Worldwide, a small group of corporations controls most of the commercial seed and agrochemical trade. Monsanto, the best known, was bought by the German firm Bayer in 2018. These companies sell seed and the chemicals designed to go with it. Many hybrid seeds do not breed true when replanted, so farmers must buy again every season. When our own varieties disappear from the hearth and the market, we lose the ability to say no. Whoever Controls Your Stomach This year has already shown us the danger. The World Bank projected that global fertiliser prices could rise by about 31 per cent in 2026. Ghana imported roughly 554,000 tonnes of fertiliser in 2024, nearly all of it from abroad. Decisions made in distant capitals and shipping lanes reached every farm in Ellembelle and Ejura within weeks. Seed can follow the same path. A bag that is cheap or free today may cost many times more in ten years, once local seed systems have collapsed and farmers have no alternative. Nobody can predict the exact price, and that uncertainty is the risk. A people that cannot plant without permission is not fully free. This is how food becomes a weapon. Sanctions, export bans and price shocks have been used against nations before. Africa, with the fastest-growing population on earth, will be the largest food market of this century. Those who own its seed will hold great power over its governments. The Silent Disappearance of Our Wildlife Ask anyone above sixty. Vultures once circled over every market, abattoir and refuse dump in our towns. Today many of our children have never seen one. Ghana has eight vulture species. Six are now of serious conservation concern, and three, the hooded, white-backed and white-headed vultures, are critically endangered. Their last secure nesting grounds are in places such as Mole National Park. Poisoning is the biggest killer. Farmers lace dead animals with farm chemicals to kill predators, and one poisoned carcass can wipe out a whole flock. Poachers poison vultures on purpose because circling birds betray their kills. The trade in vulture parts for charms, and the felling of the silk cotton trees where they nest, add to the loss. Vultures are nature's sanitation workers. They clear away dead animals before disease can spread. Where they disappear, rotting carcasses, stray dogs and rats multiply, and so does the risk of disease to people and livestock. The losses on the forest floor are just as real. Wild mushrooms and giant land snails were once free food and income for rural families after the first rains. Both are now much harder to find. In 2022 Nana Boakye Ameyaw Pentenprem II, Nifahene of the Techiman Traditional Council, warned that careless use of pesticides and weedicides had already wiped out some herbs, trees, mushrooms and snails in his area. Deforestation, bush burning and over-harvesting have played their part. Chemicals finish the job. Mushrooms grow from living networks of fungi in the soil and leaf litter, and snails lay their eggs in the soil. Ground that is soaked season after season with weedicide and insecticide cannot sustain either. We Are Wearing Out Our Land Continuous chemical farming without returning organic matter to the soil acidifies it and destroys the life that keeps it fertile. Each season more fertiliser is needed to produce the same yield. Our cocoa belt shows the result, with old, exhausted farms and falling output. Add galamsey, which has poisoned rivers and turned farmland into craters, and the scale of the loss is frightening. Land that is degraded today will not feed our grandchildren. As custodians of stool lands, chiefs carry a particular responsibility. The land was given to us by our ancestors in trust for those not yet born. What Must Be Done Government should: Establish national and district community seed banks to collect, store and multiply indigenous varieties before they are lost. Review the Plant Variety Protection Act to guarantee farmers' rights to save, share and sell seed, through a home-grown (sui generis) system suited to smallholders. Keep seed research in public Ghanaian hands, funding CSIR so that improved varieties remain affordable and royalty-free to our farmers. Enforce the existing GMO labelling guidelines so that every Ghanaian can choose what to eat. Back domestic organic fertiliser production alongside the larger chemical fertiliser projects now planned. Direct the EPA to tighten control of highly hazardous pesticides, train farmers in safe use and enforce safe disposal of containers. Make it a serious offence to poison carcasses with farm chemicals, and protect vulture nesting trees. Traditional authorities should: Set aside stool land for fallow, agroecology demonstration farms and community seed custody. Make bylaws against spraying near rivers and drinking water sources. Declare vultures and their silk cotton nesting trees protected on stool lands. Use durbars and festivals to honour farmers who keep traditional seed and soil practices alive. Farmers and the youth should: Return organic matter to the soil through compost, mulch, animal manure and crop residues. Rotate cereals with legumes such as cowpea and groundnut, which fix nitrogen naturally. Save and exchange their best seed every season. Use mechanical weeders and protective equipment, and never apply chemicals without training. Families and consumers should: Buy and eat local, whole foods and cut down on processed and sugary imports. Teach children where food comes from, and that farming is honourable work. Conclusion Our forefathers did not have tractors, laboratories or loans. They had the land, the seed and their own strength, and with these they fed generations. We have far more knowledge than they did. We must not end up with less control. The first conquest of Africa came with a book and a prayer. If we are careless, the next will come in a seed bag. Ghana must decide now who will own the seed our children plant. The decision is ours, and the time is now. By Nana Annor Amihere II For more news , join The Chronicle Newspaper channel on WhatsApp: https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VbBSs55E50UqNPvSOm2z

title: Remembering actor, comedian and media personality Kwame Dzokoto
snippet: Seth Kwame Dzokoto became widely recognised for playing Judge Koboo in Efiewura, one of Ghana’s well-known local television productions. Beyond acting, Dzokoto demonstrated his versatility as a television presenter, particularly through TV3’s food and tourism programme Edziban. The programme explored Ghanaian cuisine and local food culture, introducing audiences to different meals and culinary experiences across […]
content: Seth Kwame Dzokoto became widely recognised for playing Judge Koboo in Efiewura, one of Ghana’s well-known local television productions. Beyond acting, Dzokoto demonstrated his versatility as a television presenter, particularly through TV3’s food and tourism programme Edziban. The programme explored Ghanaian cuisine and local food culture, introducing audiences to different meals and culinary experiences across the country. His work in television, alongside his comedy and advertising voice-overs, helped build his profile as an entertainer who could connect with audiences across different formats. Broadcasting and voice-over career Dzokoto also had a career in radio, working with stations including Skyy Power FM in Takoradi and Hello FM in Kumasi. His broadcasting work complemented his television appearances and voice-over assignments, making him a familiar voice as well as a recognisable face. His career reflected a range of interests within the media industry, from comedy and acting to presenting and broadcasting. Entry into politics Outside entertainment, Dzokoto ventured into partisan politics under the banner of the National Democratic Congress (NDC). He contested the Tarkwa-Nsuaem parliamentary seat in the 2016 general election, taking his public profile beyond the entertainment industry and into electoral politics. The entertainer died on Thursday, October 22, 2026. Reports say he collapsed during a radio show at Owass Radio in the Tarkwa Nsuaem Municipality of the Western Region. He was rushed to a hospital in Tarkwa, where he was pronounced dead on arrival.

title: Ghana Calls for Global Framework to Unlock Forest Finance
snippet: At a separate panel discussion on forests and climate at the London Climate Action Week, the Deputy Minister called for a coherent international framework for jurisdictional forest carbon credits to help unlock large-scale investment in forest protection. Hon. Sulemana mentioned that Ghana's forest and climate journey had evolved from REDD+ programmes to advanced Article 6 […]
content: At a separate panel discussion on forests and climate at the London Climate Action Week, the Deputy Minister called for a coherent international framework for jurisdictional forest carbon credits to help unlock large-scale investment in forest protection. Hon. Sulemana mentioned that Ghana's forest and climate journey had evolved from REDD+ programmes to advanced Article 6 mechanisms, backed by stronger monitoring systems, safeguards and benefit-sharing arrangements. "Our ambition is clear. In our updated NDCs, Ghana has doubled the volume of emission reductions we are making available for Article 6 cooperation", he stated. The Deputy Minister urged future COP presidencies to support a coherent, predictable and trusted international framework for jurisdictional forest credits to boost investor confidence and increase demand for high-integrity forest credits. He however warned that forest conservation efforts would struggle to attract adequate financing if carbon prices fail to reflect the true cost of protecting and restoring forests. "Forest countries cannot deliver high-quality mitigation at scale if carbon prices remain disconnected from the true cost of protecting and restoring forests", he said. London Climate Action Week is an annual event that brings together political leaders, businesses, investors and environmental groups to discuss climate solutions and accelerate action ahead of major international climate negotiations. ENDS MLNR-PR UPDATES
source: Ghana Public Services (Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources)

title: Ghana Pushes for Fair and High-Integrity Carbon Markets at London Climate Action Week
snippet: Ghana has renewed its call for a fair, transparent and high-integrity global carbon market, saying it is essential for mobilising climate finance and helping developing countries meet their emissions reduction targets. Speaking at a meeting of the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets during London Climate Action Week on June 23, 2026, the Deputy Minister for […]
content: Ghana has renewed its call for a fair, transparent and high-integrity global carbon market, saying it is essential for mobilising climate finance and helping developing countries meet their emissions reduction targets. Speaking at a meeting of the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets during London Climate Action Week on June 23, 2026, the Deputy Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Honourable Yusif Sulemana, described carbon markets as a practical tool for unlocking investment, accelerating mitigation, and delivering real benefits for communities and nature. He revealed that Ghana had taken bold steps to integrate carbon markets into its national climate strategy, assigning 24 million tonnes of its emission reduction target to Article 6 cooperation under the Paris Agreement. According to him, the country has doubled that ambition in its revised Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Hon. Sulemana also highlighted Ghana's four bilateral carbon market agreements with Switzerland, Sweden, Singapore and South Korea, describing them as evidence of the country's readiness and commitment to transparency and environmental integrity. He added Ghana's focus is now on scaling investment in carbon finance projects, including clean cooking, renewable energy, forest conservation and methane reduction. "We want to see more high-quality mitigation activities," the Deputy Minister said. He, however, stressed that credibility must remain at the heart of market growth. "Integrity is the foundation of trust, and trust is the currency of carbon markets", Hon. Sulemana added. He called for fair carbon pricing and equitable benefits for host communities. ENDS MLNR-PR UPDATES
source: Ghana Public Services (Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources)

title: NAIMOS Leads Decisive Operation at Oda River Forest Reserve – Dismantles Illegal Mining Network and Arrests Armed Imposters.
snippet: The National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS), in close coordination with the Ashanti Regional Security Council (REGSEC), has carried out a successful and intelligence-driven operation that dismantled entrenched illegal mining networks within the Oda River Forest Reserve in the Ashanti Region. On 23rd October 2025, the elite NAIMOS Taskforce, working jointly with operatives from the […]
content: The National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS), in close coordination with the Ashanti Regional Security Council (REGSEC), has carried out a successful and intelligence-driven operation that dismantled entrenched illegal mining networks within the Oda River Forest Reserve in the Ashanti Region. On 23rd October 2025, the elite NAIMOS Taskforce, working jointly with operatives from the Ashanti Regional Security and with some logistical support from the Ashanti REGSEC, launched a coordinated mission that resulted in the arrest of some illegal miners and nine (9) armed imposters posing as National Security operatives. The operation, meticulously planned jointly by NAIMOS Headquarters and the Ashanti REGSEC, was aimed at restoring law and order in one of Ghana’s most environmentally degraded reserves. NAIMOS deployed three tactical teams across the forest to secure access routes and apprehend suspects. Acting on credible intelligence from local informants, operatives intercepted several illegal miners attempting to flee the reserve on motorbikes. Fifteen were arrested after admitting that they had been warned about the taskforce’s approach. During the operation, NAIMOS officers also encountered nine armed men dressed in khaki uniforms who falsely identified themselves as National Security personnel. Upon interrogation, the suspects claimed to be acting under the command of a certain Major Jabari. A search of the men uncovered one pistol with three rounds of ammunition, one toy pistol, one pump-action shotgun with three cartridges, two handcuffs, and eight pouches, all of which were seized as exhibits for further investigation. In a separate development, NAIMOS intelligence operatives foiled an attempted bribery by individuals who arrived in a Toyota Tundra and a Ram pickup, claiming they were associates of the arrested illegal miners. The men approached the taskforce under the pretext of “greeting” the officers and “pleading” for the release of their associates. During the engagement, they offered GH₵100,000 as a bribe and an additional GH₵20,000 as “chop money.” The operatives, acting with tactical restraint and professionalism, feigned interest before arresting the suspects for attempting to bribe law enforcement officers. Following the arrests, the taskforce proceeded deeper into the Oda River Forest Reserve to assess the extent of environmental damage. The once reclaimed forest, previously replanted with trees and palm trees, had been severely destroyed by renewed illegal mining. Vast tracts of land were found degraded, vegetation cleared, and water bodies heavily polluted. Further inspection revealed that illegal miners had established a makeshift settlement deep within the reserve, consisting of numerous wooden structures and tents serving as living quarters and operational bases. The taskforce, acting under environmental protection directives, dismantled and set the illegal structures and equipment ablaze to prevent future reoccupation. Throughout the mission, NAIMOS officers exhibited exceptional discipline, professionalism, and integrity in the face of armed resistance, deceit, and attempted corruption. In similar fashion, another NAIMOS taskforce, currently operating in the Western North Region, concurrently patrolled and raided illegal mining sites at Oda Ahenkro in the Amenfi West District. During the raids illegal mining activities were disrupted in the area and several makeshift structures and equipment were destroyed or seized by the NAIMOS task force The successful operations, especially the one at Oda River Forest Reserve represents a significant milestone in Ghana’s ongoing fight against illegal mining, made possible through the strategic collaboration between NAIMOS and the Ashanti Regional Security Council, whose coordination and logistical support ensured operational success. Director of Operations of NAIMOS, Colonel Dominic Buah, commended the joint effort, describing the mission as “a model of inter-agency cooperation and enforcement excellence.” “No individual, group, or impostor will be allowed to exploit Ghana’s natural resources with impunity,” Colonel Buah stated. “Through sustained partnerships with the Regional Security Councils, NAIMOS will continue to identify, dismantle, and neutralize illegal mining operations across the country to protect our forests and water bodies for future generations.” END
source: Ghana Public Services (Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources)

title: Ghana has begun discussions with Rosatom on first nuclear power station – Mahama
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has announced that Ghana has initiated discussions with the Russian State Nuclear Energy Corporation, Rosatom, toward the establishment of the country's first nuclear power station.
content: President John Mahama President John Dramani Mahama has announced that Ghana has initiated discussions with the Russian State Nuclear Energy Corporation, Rosatom, toward the establishment of the country's first nuclear power station. Speaking at the Third Russia-Africa Forum in Moscow, President Mahama highlighted the critical role of reliable electricity in Africa's development. The President identified inadequate electric power as one of the major obstacles to Africa's progress, stressing that industrialisation required reliable and affordable energy to succeed. "We have initiated discussions with Rosatom on the establishment of Ghana's first nuclear power station," adding that Russia had a comparative advantage in the field of renewable energy and nuclear power – an area where Russia and Africa's cooperation could yield tangible results. He noted that Ghana had a historical relationship with Russia in the peaceful use of nuclear energy, recalling that as far back as 1964, the Soviet Union provided Ghana with a two-megawatt nuclear reactor for scientific and research purposes. President Mahama stated that several Ghanaian nuclear scientists were trained in Russia to operate the reactor. The announcement signals a significant step in Ghana's long-standing ambition to add nuclear power to its energy mix, as the demand for electricity grows with industrial expansion and population growth. A nuclear power station would provide baseload capacity to complement the country's existing hydropower and thermal generation sources. President Mahama's remarks underscore the broader case for strengthened Russia-Africa cooperation in the energy sector, with Moscow positioned as a partner in both renewable energy and nuclear technology. The President said such cooperation could deliver concrete results for the continent's industrialisation drive. Source: GNA

title: President Mahama hails Russia’s ‘historical solidarity’ with Africa
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has delivered a personal and historically grounded address at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin and all Russians for decades of support to the African continent.
content: President John Mahama (seated middle) President John Dramani Mahama has delivered a personal and historically grounded address at the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin and all Russians for decades of support to the African continent. He also cited his own experience as a scholarship student in the former Soviet Union as proof of that enduring friendship. Speaking at the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, President Mahama said the relationship between Russia and Africa was forged during the struggles against colonialism and apartheid, and he made an explicit appeal for continued partnership grounded in that history. President Mahama noted that Russia stood by Africa during the struggle against colonialism and extended support to the newly independent African countries. He highlighted education as a central pillar of the relationship, noting that Russia had trained thousands of African professionals. “You educated and provided skills training to thousands of African students over the years … to help in the development of our countries,” he said. He also cited Russia’s opposition to white minority rule in South Africa, stating that “Moscow stood by Africa and expressed solidarity and material support during the fight against apartheid,” saying Russia had been a true and selfless friend of Africa for decades. President Mahama that noted next year, Ghana would celebrate 70 years of its independence as a first sub-Saharan African country to break free from colonial domination, and on this occasion the country wished to salute Russia for its solidarity in the decolonisation of the African continent. He said “Our interactions and discussions since yesterday reveal many opportunities for expanding the relations between Russia and Africa in the areas of trade and investment," reiterating that Africa was the continent of the future. He underscored that opportunities abound for mutual investment by African and Russian investors in the areas of agriculture, agro-processing, healthcare, energy, security, and digital services. President Mahama said Ghana approached these discussions guided by a tradition of non-alignment, respect for sovereignty, equality, and a commitment to peaceful international cooperation. "We seek friendship with all countries and partnerships that advance our development priorities, trade between Africa and Russia has considerable room to grow, both in volume and in the range of goods exchanged," President Mahama said. "Our task is to remove the practical barriers that prevent businesses from translating goodwill into lasting commercial relationships." He noted that Ghana offered opportunities in cocoa, cashew, shell nuts, horticulture, mineral processing, and manufacturing, stating that the nation's institutions and its strategic location on the Gulf of Guinea provided a foundation for investment. Again, as host of the Secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), Ghana was also well placed to support businesses seeking opportunities across the continent, the President said. President Mahama said in accordance with the agreements, rules, and implementation arrangements, they were inviting Russian businesses to work with Ghanaian counterparts in agro-processing, fertilizer production, agricultural machinery, pharmaceuticals, energy, transport infrastructure, and the digital economy. He said joint ventures should build local expertise and create opportunities for small and medium-sized businesses alongside large investors. “We must also improve access for African products to enter Russian markets, and that better market information, predictable standards, stronger logistics, and closer cooperation between our business communities can make trade more balanced and more rewarding for both sides," President Mahama stated. The Third Russia-Africa Summit, held between October 28–29, gathered African leaders to discuss economic, humanitarian, and security cooperation with Moscow. Source: GNA

title: RUDN University confers honorary doctorate degree on President Mahama
snippet: The Patrice Lumumba Peoples' Friendship University of Russia (RUDN University) in Moscow on Tuesday conferred an honorary doctorate degree on President John Dramani Mahama.
content: The Patrice Lumumba Peoples' Friendship University of Russia (RUDN University) in Moscow on Tuesday conferred an honorary doctorate degree on President John Dramani Mahama. The award ceremony, which was led by Professor Oleg A. Yastrebov, RUDN Rector, was in recognition of President Mahama's commitment towards expanding access to education and strengthening Ghana-Russian relations in the area of education and scientific research. President Mahama, who is an alumnus of RUDN is in Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit. President Mahama in his acceptance speech said, he accepted the honorary doctorate degree as encouragement to continue working for education and peaceful cooperation among people. He said, he also received it as a reminder that leadership must remain open to continuous learning. To the leadership, faculty, staff, and students of Patrice Lumumba University, the President offered his sincere thanks. "I shall cherish this honour and the friendship it represents. I am pleased to be an honorary graduate of Patrice Lumumba University, and I will carry this honour with pride," President Mahama said. "May your institution continue to bring people together in the pursuit of knowledge. "May the ties between Ghana and Russia create further opportunities for our young people, and may the learning achieved within these walls find its fullest expression in service to humanity." President Mahama said the Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia was a symbol of the solidarity and friendship shown by the people of the Soviet Union and Russia to countries newly emerged from colonialism in Africa. He said the Institute over several decades opened its doors to thousands of African students, who drank from its fountain of knowledge and returned to help build their newly liberated nations. He noted that the idea of a university devoted to friendship among peoples continues to speak directly to the needs of their time. He said at RUDN, students from different nations and backgrounds could encounter one another as classmates, as colleagues, and, most importantly, as friends, adding that they learn that understanding another culture requires one to be curious, to be patient, and to exercise respect. President Mahama reiterated that these relationships matter even more today because they live in a world troubled by conflict and mistrust. He said academic cooperation keeps channels of conversation and dialogue open and that it allows people to work together on problems that no one country could solve alone—from public health and food security to energy and climate change. "For Ghana, education is central to our development ambitions. Our young population must have the opportunity to acquire knowledge and use it productively," President Mahama said. President Mahama underscored that a talented young person should not lose the chance to study because their family couls not afford the cost. He said over the years, progressive policies such as Free Compulsory Universal Basic Education and the School Feeding Programme had ensured gender parity and almost total enrolment in Ghana's basic education programmes. He said additional initiatives such as the Free Senior High School programme, the No-Fee Stress policy, support for students with disabilities, and improved access to financing for tertiary students has all helped remove financial barriers that prevent young Ghanaians from accessing education. President Mahama reiterated that the Government was also committed to strengthening technical and vocational training, scientific research, and digital skills. He said expanding access must go hand in hand with improving quality and ensuring that what students learn equips them for the demands of work and citizenship. President Mahama said a university qualification should give its holder the confidence to ask searching questions and the ability to solve real-world problems. "For our country, the value of education shows up in better healthcare, more productive agriculture, stronger businesses, and public institutions that serve our people well," President Mahama stated. "This is why closer relationships among universities, industry, and Governments are essential." He noted that research must have pathways into practice, and students need opportunities to test their ideas, gain experience, and turn their abilities into livelihoods. President Mahama said, he therefore welcomes the discussion he had had with Professor Yastrebov and his proposal for the establishment of a Russian–African studies programme. "I also note your kind invitation to send some of our brightest students to Patrice Lumumba University for specialization." President Mahama further expressed his appreciation to the Russian Government for the scholarships extended to Ghanaian students and for its continued support for educational cooperation. He also thanked the University, the Rector, the lecturers, and the host communities that had helped Ghanaian students settle and gain a valuable education far away from home. Source: GNA

title: Christ Apostolic Church receives 1,500 bags of fertiliser under Feed Ghana Programme
snippet: The Christ Apostolic Church International (CACI) has received 1,500 bags of fertiliser valued at more than GH¢700,000 under the Government’s Feed Ghana Programme to support institutional farming and boost agricultural production.
content: The Christ Apostolic Church International (CACI) has received 1,500 bags of fertiliser valued at more than GH¢700,000 under the Government’s Feed Ghana Programme to support institutional farming and boost agricultural production. The donation forms part of a component of the programme aimed at encouraging institutions, including faith-based organisations, to engage in crop production and increase food output. The Feed Ghana Programme is a four-year national agricultural transformation initiative covering 2025 to 2028. It was launched by President John Dramani Mahama on April 12, 2025, in Techiman. The programme is a flagship pillar of the broader Agriculture for Economic Transformation Agenda (AETA), which seeks to reduce food imports, increase domestic production, and create jobs. Mr Gordon Asubongteng, Deputy Feed Ghana Coordinator in charge of Institutions at the Ministry of Food and Agriculture (MoFA), said the programme’s interventions would contribute to national food security. He said the Government had increased investment in the programme to attract more people, particularly the youth, into crop production. Investments had also been made in mechanisation and Farmer Service Centres to support agricultural activities. Mr Asubongteng said the fertiliser donation was part of government's support for faith-based organisations to promote agriculture, following similar interventions for the Ghana Prisons Service and other security services. “We want to tell CACI that we are prepared to work with them to achieve something good for the nation. They should be able to improve production so that it will benefit everybody in Ghana,” he said. He said the Ministry was encouraging farmers to form cooperatives based on their agricultural activities, explaining that such groups could help reduce smuggling and facilitate the transfer of knowledge and technology among farmers. Apostle Samuel Amponsah-Frimpong, Chairman of the Christ Apostolic Church International, commended the Government for the support, describing the donation as a demonstration of the partnership between the Church and the government to create jobs and empower people. He said the support had come at an opportune time, during the minor planting season, and assured the public that the fertiliser would be distributed transparently to farmers across the regions. “As a church, our vision is not only to feed the soul but also to feed the nation. This initiative aligns perfectly with our agricultural development programme, which seeks to make our members productive and self-reliant,” Apostle Amponsah-Frimpong said. Source: GNA

title: From family tradition to market competition: What makes brands endure in Ghana
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has described Nestlé Ghana Limited as an institution deeply woven into the lives of generations of Ghanaians, recalling how Ideal Milk, alongside Milo, Cerelac, Nescafé and Carnation, had become familiar products in households across the country.
content: President John Mahama President John Dramani Mahama has described Nestlé Ghana Limited as an institution deeply woven into the lives of generations of Ghanaians, recalling how Ideal Milk, alongside Milo, Cerelac, Nescafé and Carnation, had become familiar products in households across the country. Speaking at the commissioning of a new evaporated milk production line at the company’s Tema factory on October 8, 2026, the president drew on childhood memories of Ideal Milk in tea, koko, rice water and other meals to illustrate the enduring relationship between the company’s brands and Ghanaian families. His remarks highlighted more than nostalgia. They raised a broader question about the strength of established consumer brands in a market where household spending is growing, but many brands continue to struggle to reach a wider section of the population. For manufacturers, retailers, and marketers, the challenge is not simply to maintain familiarity or generate higher sales. It is to remain relevant to consumers’ changing needs while attracting new households. Findings from Worldpanel by Numerator’s Brand Footprint research suggest that even in a growing market, increased spending does not necessarily translate into wider consumer reach. Ghana’s fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) market recorded a 12.9 per cent increase in household spending in 2025, reflecting continued consumer activity. Yet 82 per cent of the country’s top 250 FMCG brands reached fewer than half of Ghanaian households. The contrast reveals a significant gap between spending growth and household penetration. Although consumers spent more on everyday products, most leading brands had not achieved broad reach across the country’s households. For businesses, this raises an important question: are brands growing because more households are choosing them, or because existing customers are spending more? Spending more does not always mean reaching more people The research found that 69 per cent of Ghana’s top 250 FMCG brands recorded higher consumer spending in 2025, while only 52 per cent increased their Consumer Reach Points (CRPs). Mr Ifedayo Akinyele, Country Manager of Worldpanel by Numerator, Ghana, said the figures showed that “value growth is currently more widespread than growth in consumer choice”. The distinction matters because higher spending can result from existing customers buying more frequently during each shopping occasion or choosing different product combinations. Such changes can improve a brand’s sales performance without necessarily expanding the number of households buying it. Consumer Reach Points (CRPs) measure both the number of households purchasing a brand and how frequently they buy it. An increase in CRPs, therefore, does not automatically mean that a brand has attracted more households. The research suggests that sustainable growth requires businesses to assess both the value generated by existing customers and their ability to attract new buyers. Mr Phillip Ofulue, Account Director at Worldpanel by Numerator Ghana, said Ghanaian consumers remained conscious of the value they received from each purchase. “Growth cannot rely on higher spending alone. Brands must remain relevant, reach more shoppers and give them compelling reasons to choose them again,” he said. Local and regional brands command consumer choices Another notable finding is the strong position of local and regional brands in Ghana’s consumer market. According to the research, these brands accounted for 84 per cent of consumer choices among the country’s top 250 FMCG brands. Although the findings do not establish a single reason for their performance, factors such as familiarity, relevance to local tastes, affordability and availability may help explain their place in everyday purchasing routines. Their performance highlights the importance of understanding the circumstances in which consumers make purchasing decisions. A brand may be well known, but its ability to remain part of a household’s regular shopping choices can depend on whether consumers can afford it, find it easily and consider it suitable for their needs. For businesses seeking to expand their reach, these considerations are particularly important beyond major urban centres, where distribution and product accessibility can influence whether consumers can choose particular brands. Brands that illustrate different paths to growth The research offers examples of how established and growing brands compete for consumer attention. Nestlé’s Milo retained its position as Ghana’s most chosen FMCG brand in 2025, recording 245.3 million Consumer Reach Points. Its performance was supported by its strong position in the cocoa beverage category, which the research identified as the country’s second most frequently purchased FMCG category. The average shopper, according to the findings, purchased from the category at least once a week, as Milo accounted for almost 90 per cent of sales within the category. The research also reported that the brand maintained a presence in nearly every Ghanaian household. Onga ranked second among the most chosen brands, with 226.7 million consumer choices, supported by its position in the seasoning category. Kivo, meanwhile, climbed seven places to third position after more than doubling its consumer reach points to 161.9 million. Its growth was associated with an expanding buyer base, a presence across multiple food categories, and accessible pack sizes and price points. Seasoning was particularly important to its performance, with the brand accounting for about 85 per cent of sales within one segment of the category. The contrasting performances of Milo and Kivo illustrate two important aspects of brand competition: maintaining a strong position among existing consumers and expanding the number of households that choose a product. The research further found that among brands that increased their CRPs by more than 2.5 per cent, approximately 62 per cent achieved growth through a combination of household penetration and purchase frequency. This suggests that attracting new buyers while retaining existing ones can be an important route to stronger brand performance. What the numbers really say about Ghanaian shoppers The data portrays a highly competitive market in which brands must continually earn their place in consumers’ baskets. What it demonstrates is that accessibility, relevance and consumer reach remain important drivers of performance. Brands that continue to attract households and remain part of regular purchasing routines appear better positioned for growth. At the same time, caution is necessary when interpreting consumer behaviour. The findings do not establish that specific purchasing changes are being driven solely by household budget pressures. Nor do they prove the extent to which factors such as price sensitivity, brand switching or pack-size changes are shaping consumer decisions. Those questions would require additional consumer behaviour research. The strategic challenge for manufacturers and retailers For manufacturers and retailers, the findings suggest that growth cannot be reduced to a single lever. Price increases may improve value performance, but they do not necessarily increase the number of households buying a brand. Likewise, wider distribution alone may not be enough if products lack relevance to local needs and purchasing realities. The most effective growth strategies are likely to combine multiple interconnected elements: pricing, pack architecture, distribution, accessibility, consumer recruitment, and purchase frequency. The challenge becomes especially important outside major urban centres, where availability, accessibility and relevance continue to shape brand reach. Brands seeking broader penetration must ensure products are available where consumers shop, offered in formats that fit purchasing realities and positioned in ways that resonate with local consumption needs. The opportunity beyond higher spending The most important insight from Ghana’s FMCG market is not that households are spending more. It is that spending growth alone is an incomplete measure of success. With 82 per cent of the country’s top 250 FMCG brands still reaching fewer than half of households, significant penetration headroom remains available. The evidence also suggests that the strongest-performing brands combine household recruitment with stronger engagement among existing buyers. For Ghana’s manufacturers, retailers and marketers, the challenge is therefore clear. Sustainable growth will come not simply from extracting more value from the same consumers but from giving more households a reason and an opportunity to choose a brand in the first place, and then enough value to choose it again. The brands that master both sides of that equation are likely to define the next chapter of growth in Ghana’s FMCG market. President Mahama’s recollection of products that have featured in Ghanaian family life for generations provides a reminder of the value of that connection. Market research, meanwhile, points to the challenge of sustaining it in a competitive consumer environment. Ultimately, a brand’s place in family life is valuable, but enduring market strength depends on continuing to earn the consumer’s choice. By Philcollins Duah Frimpong Source: GNA

title: Cancer patients benefit from Ghana Medical Trust Fund – Surgeon
snippet: Dr Victor Dassah, a Surgeon at the Upper East Regional Hospital, has commended the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) for extending its support to cancer patients.
content: Dr Victor Dassah – Surgeon – Upper East Regional Hospital. Dr Victor Dassah, a Surgeon at the Upper East Regional Hospital, has commended the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) for extending its support to cancer patients. He noted that the Fund eased the financial and emotional burden associated with cancer treatment, and said the support brought relief to patients who previously struggled to access further treatment due to financial difficulties. Speaking on the impact of the GMTF, at a soiree for partners, specialists and management of the hospital, organized by the GMTF in Bolgatanga, the Surgeon disclosed that the hospital had so far enrolled 14 breast cancer patients and one prostate cancer patient onto the Fund. “I want to thank management of the Fund extensively. I have a personal experience with cancer, and it is not easy being a cancer patient or a relative of a cancer patient. The financial, psychological and other challenges are enormous,” he said. Dr Dassah expressed appreciation to the Fund for including cancer care in its programmes, describing the support as a significant intervention for patients who would otherwise struggle to finance their treatment. According to him, some patients had delayed seeking further treatment for several months, while others had waited close to a year because they could not afford the cost of care. “One patient had been coming to the hospital for almost a year but, because of financial difficulties, she was unable to proceed with further treatment. However, about a month ago, she was enrolled onto the programme, and since then, approvals have been given for her management and treatment plan,” the Surgeon said. Dr Dassah noted that the GMTF, popularly known as MahamaCares, had restored hope among beneficiaries, many of whom he said expressed gratitude for the assistance they received. The Surgeon emphasized that the financial burden of healthcare could be overwhelming even for medical professionals and stressed the need for healthcare providers to appreciate the difficulties patients face when required to pay for medicines, investigations and treatment. “Even as a medical person, if I must go somewhere to pay my own medical bills, it is not easy for me. So, imagine somebody who is not in the medical profession and may not have the means to pay,” Dr Dassah said. He further commended management of the Fund for improving the patient enrolment process, saying the process, which previously took considerable time, had become faster. “Initially, it usually took some time before many of these patients were enrolled. But these days, the last patient I enrolled was processed in less than a few hours. Things have really changed, and in most cases, patients are enrolled in less than 24 hours,” the Surgeon disclosed. Despite the progress, the Surgeon appealed to the Fund and relevant stakeholders to support the hospital to address infrastructure and diagnostic gaps that continued to affect comprehensive cancer care. He said the hospital could take biopsies but lacked the capacity to conduct histopathological examinations locally, which forced patients to seek such services at other facilities. He noted that the situation increased the burden on patients and resulted in the loss of potential revenue to the hospital through referrals. He further disclosed that the hospital had oncology specialists willing to administer chemotherapy but was yet to establish the necessary capacity to commence the service due to institutional challenges and called for support to strengthen the hospital’s cancer management services, particularly histopathology and chemotherapy, to enable patients to receive more comprehensive care at the facility. “We are hoping the Fund will help us structure our cancer management so that we would not have to refer cases we diagnose here. We have the manpower for most of the treatments, but we need the necessary support and facilities,” Dr Dassah said. He expressed optimism that addressing the gaps would improve access to timely cancer diagnosis and treatment, reduce the financial burden on patients and strengthen the hospital’s capacity to provide specialized healthcare services. Source: GNA

title: Mahama Seeks Russian Investment In Energy Sector
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has expressed Ghana’s interest in strengthening energy cooperation with Russia, particularly in solar and nuclear power, ahead of a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He said the meeting, expected on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit, would provide an opportunity to explore new areas of cooperation in energy, investment […]
content: President John Dramani Mahama has expressed Ghana’s interest in strengthening energy cooperation with Russia, particularly in solar and nuclear power, ahead of a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He said the meeting, expected on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit, would provide an opportunity to explore new areas of cooperation in energy, investment and broader economic relations. President Mahama, who was speaking during one of the engagements in Russia, said Ghana was looking to deepen its historic relations with Russia and restore cooperation between the two countries to previous levels. “The unity between Ghana and Russia is one that is historic, and we believe that the time has come for us to bring it back to that level,” he said. He explained that Ghana was exploring alternative energy sources, including solar power and nuclear energy, to diversify its energy mix, noting that Russia had advanced technology in those areas. “Ghana is one of the leading producers of power. We export power to Togo, Burkina Faso, Benin and we exchange power with Cote d’Ivoire,” he said. The President said Ghana’s interest in alternative energy sources presented opportunities for collaboration with Russia, particularly in the development of nuclear power and renewable energy. President John Dramani Mahama He expressed optimism that his planned bilateral engagement with President Putin would help strengthen relations between the two countries and create opportunities for investment and economic cooperation. “And I’m sure that after the meeting, it will draw our relations even closer in terms of investments and in terms of economic relations,” he said. President Mahama said his decision to personally attend the Russia-Africa Summit reflected Ghana’s commitment to revitalising its relationship with Russia and pursuing mutually beneficial partnerships. The proposed engagement comes as Ghana explores options to diversify its energy sources and strengthen its electricity supply through alternative technologies. title: SA’s Evacuation Ruckus: Why Is Okudzeto Still In Office? … Samuel Jinapor Asks; Urges President Mahama To Sack Him If He Fails To Resign
snippet: The Ranking Member on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has called on the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, to resign immediately over alleged financial irregularities in the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa. He has also asked President Mahama to terminate the minister’s appointment if he failed to voluntary resign, […]
content: The Ranking Member on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has called on the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, to resign immediately over alleged financial irregularities in the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa. He has also asked President Mahama to terminate the minister’s appointment if he failed to voluntary resign, citing Article 81(a) of the 1992 Constitution. “Given the gravity of these revelations and in order to ensure an impartial investigation into the matter, we call on the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, to resign immediately,” the Minority Caucus said at a news conference in Accra yesterday. Mr Samuel Abu Jinapor addressing the media in Parliament yesterday The caucus said the evacuation exercise cost GH¢49,721,786 according to figures announced by the minister. It said an examination of documents obtained from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs through a request under the Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989) had revealed discrepancies between the minister’s claims and the payment registers. According to the Minority, the documents showed duplicated entries, gaps in supporting records and expenditure requiring further explanation. “Those further enquiries have uncovered additional grave anomalies and disturbing contradictions that deepen our suspicions about the handling of these public funds,” the statement said. It also cited media investigations, which reportedly uncovered cases of evacuees who did not receive their allowances, duplicate entries, payments recorded without signatures and expenditure for which supporting receipts were unavailable. “The evidence before us reveals grave financial irregularities, compelling indications of the misapplication of public funds and possible fraud,” the caucus said. The Minority consequently reiterated its call for a comprehensive independent audit of the evacuation exercise by “an internationally reputable accounting firm with a proven track record and unquestionable integrity.” It argued that Mr Ablakwa’s handling of the exercise had brought his office into disrepute and cited Section 2.1(j) of President John Dramani Mahama’s 2025 Code of Conduct and Ethics for Political Appointees, which it said required resignation where a minister’s actions or leadership resulted in significant failure, corruption or a breach of public trust. The caucus further called on President Mahama to terminate the minister’s appointment if he failed to resign, citing Article 81(a) of the 1992 Constitutio n . It said it would also consider initiating parliamentary proceedings for a vote of censure against the minister under Article 82 of the Constitution and Order 138 of Parliament’s Standing Orders if he remained in office. The Minority denied allegations that it had paid or persuaded some evacuees to speak against the government, insisting that it had neither engaged nor paid any of them to do so. It said some evacuees had spoken voluntarily after learning of differences between what they believed they were entitled to receive and what they actually received. The caucus also cited media reports that the Ghana High Commission in Pretoria had warned evacuees against speaking to the media, questioning the need for such a warning if the authorities had nothing to hide. title: President Mahama backs Ethiopia’s bid to host 2028 AFCON
snippet: President John Dramani Mahama has backed Ethiopia’s bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), saying the country has the facilities to stage a successful tournament. Mahama made the remarks after inspecting the 52,000-capacity Bahir Dar Stadium alongside Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and other African leaders during the 12th Tana High-Level Forum […]
content: President John Dramani Mahama has backed Ethiopia’s bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), saying the country has the facilities to stage a successful tournament. Mahama made the remarks after inspecting the 52,000-capacity Bahir Dar Stadium alongside Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and other African leaders during the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. He described the stadium as impressive and noted that it had already received certification from the Confederation of African Football (CAF). “This is a very impressive stadium, 52,000 capacity stadium and it’s CAF certified already and we know that Ethiopia is putting in a bid for the African Cup of Nations 2028,” Mahama said. “Ethiopia hasn’t hosted it for a very long time so I think it’s only fair that they should be given an opportunity to do that but the facilities are impressive and I think that Ethiopia is ready to host a successful tournament.” Ethiopia last hosted AFCON in 1976, when the tournament featured eight teams. The country is now seeking another opportunity to stage Africa’s premiers men’s football competition. Credit: citisportsonline.com

title: Ghana's elections of 7 December 2016: A post-mortem
snippet: Ghana went to presidential and parliamentary polls on 7 December 2016, leading to the defeat of President John Mahama and the National Democratic Congress government by the opposition, the New Patriotic Party led by Nana Akufo-Addo. The outcome of the elections therefore followed in the same vein as those held in Ghana in 2000 and 2008, in which the incumbent party lost to the opposition. This article is based on a desk study review of the 2016 elections. There is a brief overview of the state of affairs in Ghana's electoral politics, followed by a discussion of Ghana's electoral reforms, the organisation and management of the elections, the candidates and the campaigns, and the outcome of the elections, as well as some of the challenges that faced the transition process. © 2017 The South African Institute of International Affairs.

title: Availabilty of energy and agricultural mechanization in Ghana
snippet: A variety of definitions have been postulated for food security. The bottom line, however, is the availability of food of good quality at an affordable cost to all and at all times. Many approaches have been adopted to achieve an increase in the availability of food. These include among others increased use of mechanization to expand area under cultivation. Many developing countries have adopted agricultural mechanization to modernize and speed up the process of agricultural land expansion. The available land in Ghana that is suitable for mechanization is put at 8 million hectares for which an estimated energy input of 6 × 106 kW is required. Of this amount only 3.1% is available. Analysis have shown that out of the 1.6 million hectares of land currently under mechanized cultivation the required energy input is 12 × 105 kW out of which only 15.6% is available. This shows a wide gap between the energy required and what is available to meet the objectives of agricultural mechanization.
