title: Sakumono: Uncle, niece shot dead in alleged GH¢500K debt dispute
snippet: Police are investigating the murder of two persons, identified as 47-year-old Irene Atubiga, and George Atubiga, 57, at NTHC Estate in Sakumono, following an alleged dispute over a GH¢500,000 debt. The two were reportedly shot dead on Friday, October 30, 2026, after a confrontation at their residence involving a suspect identified as Samuel Christopher Osei […]
content: Police are investigating the murder of two persons, identified as 47-year-old Irene Atubiga, and George Atubiga, 57, at NTHC Estate in Sakumono, following an alleged dispute over a GH¢500,000 debt. The two were reportedly shot dead on Friday, October 30, 2026, after a confrontation at their residence involving a suspect identified as Samuel Christopher Osei Anto. In a statement issued on Friday, the Accra Regional Police Command said preliminary investigations suggest that the incident stemmed from a financial dispute involving George Atubiga, who had allegedly borrowed GH¢500,000 from the suspect but failed to repay the money. According to the Police, the suspect, accompanied by a woman identified as Beatrice Mumuni, went to the victims’ residence on the morning of the incident to demand repayment. A misunderstanding reportedly ensued, during which the suspect allegedly shot and killed George Atubiga and his niece, Irene Atubiga. The victims were rushed to a hospital, where a medical officer pronounced them dead. Their bodies have since been deposited at the Police Hospital Mortuary for preservation and autopsy. The Baatsona Divisional Police Command is investigating the incident, while the Accra Regional Police Command says efforts are underway to apprehend the suspect. The Police have appealed to anyone with relevant information to assist with investigations. Read Also: ‘We'll pursue justice’ – Ablakwa assures family of Ghanaian teen killed in US

title: ‘We'll pursue justice’ – Ablakwa assures family of Ghanaian teen killed in US
snippet: Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has assured the family of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Javits Frimpong that the government will pursue justice following his fatal shooting in the Bronx, New York. Mr Ablakwa gave the assurance during a telephone conversation with the victim’s father, Thomas Frimpong, on Friday, October 30, 2026, during which he conveyed […]
content: Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has assured the family of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Javits Frimpong that the government will pursue justice following his fatal shooting in the Bronx, New York. Mr Ablakwa gave the assurance during a telephone conversation with the victim’s father, Thomas Frimpong, on Friday, October 30, 2026, during which he conveyed the condolences of President John Dramani Mahama and pledged the government’s support to the bereaved family. “We will pursue justice, and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it,” Mr Ablakwa told the father, according to a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Speaking on behalf of the President, the Minister also expressed the government’s grief over the teenager’s death. “We are all saddened. We are all distraught. He did not deserve this,” he said. The Ministry said officials from Ghana’s Permanent Mission in New York had also visited the family at their residence on Friday to express their condolences and solidarity. It condemned the killing and called on the relevant authorities in the Bronx to conduct a thorough investigation and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice. The Ministry further indicated that it, together with Ghana’s Permanent Mission in New York, would actively pursue the matter in collaboration with US authorities and provide the family with the necessary legal and consular assistance. The government also extended its condolences to Javits’ mother, Doris Adu Gyamfi, who is in Kumasi, as well as his friends and other relatives in Ghana and the United States. Police are searching for three men suspected of involvement in the shooting, which occurred at about 9:20 a.m. on Thursday, October 29, as Javits was on his way to school. The teenager, who moved to the United States from Ghana about a year ago, was reportedly shot in the abdomen and later died at a hospital.

title: JUSAG declares indefinite strike over salary review
snippet: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has declared an indefinite strike from Monday, November 2, 2026, over the government's failure to approve the proposed review of salaries and related allowances for Judicial Service staff. The association says the industrial action will continue until its demands are met, directing all Judicial Service staff to […]
content: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has declared an indefinite strike from Monday, November 2, 2026, over the government's failure to approve the proposed review of salaries and related allowances for Judicial Service staff. The association says the industrial action will continue until its demands are met, directing all Judicial Service staff to stay away from work from Monday. Addressing staff and the media on Friday, October 30, JUSAG General Secretary, Abdulai Yakubu, said the government had failed to meet the deadline set by the association for approval of the revised conditions of service. He maintained that the government's handling of the matter demonstrated a lack of commitment to addressing the concerns of Judicial Service workers. “By the development, therefore, and by the resolution of the Council of JUSAG, we hereby declare an indefinite strike starting from Monday, the 2nd of November, 2026,” he announced. Mr Yakubu also advised members of the public with cases scheduled for Monday not to report to court, as staff would not be available to attend to them. He said the association had made several attempts since December 2025 to secure approval for the 2026 salary review, but those efforts had yielded no results. “You may recall that on the 23rd of October 2026, the Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana notified the National Labour Commission of our intention to embark on an indefinite strike owing to the failure of the government to approve our conditions of service as recommended by the Judicial Council,” he said. Mr Yakubu explained that under Article 149 and Regulation 25 of the Judicial Service Terms and Conditions of Service Regulations, 2025 (C.I. 141), the President determines the salaries and conditions of service of Judicial Service staff based on advice from the Judicial Council, with salaries reviewed annually. He said JUSAG submitted its proposal to the Judicial Council in December 2025, after which the Council completed its work and forwarded its recommendations to the President for approval. However, he said delays in securing presidential approval compelled the association to send several reminders to the relevant authorities, warning that continued delays could threaten industrial harmony within the Judicial Service. Mr Yakubu said appeals had also been made during the association's Second Quadrennial Delegates Conference in Tamale, where the Chief of Staff assured members that the matter would be taken up with the Office of the President for expedited approval. He added that subsequent appeals during engagements involving the Chief Justice and at the recently held AMJG Conference at Labadi had also failed to produce the desired outcome. According to him, the growing frustration among members prompted JUSAG's National Executive Council to hold an emergency meeting, at which it resolved to demand approval of the Judicial Council's recommendations by October 30, 2026. The association also demanded that the approved salaries be paid in November 2026, together with arrears covering January to October. Mr Yakubu said the association formally notified the National Labour Commission on October 23 of its intention to embark on an indefinite strike if the demands were not met by the deadline. The notification was also copied to the Minister responsible for Jobs, Labour Relations and Employment, the Finance Minister, the Attorney-General, the Executive Secretary to the Office of the President and the Judicial Secretary. He criticised the Ministry of Labour for failing to act promptly on the National Labour Commission's directive to convene a meeting with relevant stakeholders to expedite the approval process.

title: Gov’t has introduced 22 laws in 18 months to protect reforms – Ato Forson
snippet: The Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, has stated that the government has introduced about 22 laws in the past 18 months as part of efforts to institutionalise its reforms and protect them from being easily reversed by future administrations. He said the legislative measures were intended to give key policy decisions a lasting […]
content: The Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, has stated that the government has introduced about 22 laws in the past 18 months as part of efforts to institutionalise its reforms and protect them from being easily reversed by future administrations. He said the legislative measures were intended to give key policy decisions a lasting legal foundation, arguing that reforms could be changed by successive governments if they were not backed by law. Dr Forson was speaking during a New Economy engagement at the University of Ghana on Friday, October 30, 2026, where he was asked how the government could ensure that its policies and reform agenda would survive changes in political leadership. The question was posed by Professor Fred Dzanku, Head of the Economics Division at the university’s Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER), who asked how “some of these brilliant policies and agenda” could be institutionalised. In response, Dr Forson said his experience in Parliament and government had shaped his approach to ensuring policy continuity. “I try to introduce a lot of laws. For the last 18 months, we've introduced about 22 laws. We are trying to put these things in law, repealing some and making amendments that require a two-thirds majority, so that we are locking in the progress,” he said. He explained that governments could easily reverse policies that had not been entrenched in legislation, making legal backing important to sustaining reforms beyond the tenure of the administration that introduced them. “Most times, it is very easy for a government of the day to change policy if you don't have it in law,” he said. Dr Forson cited amendments to the Public Financial Management Act as part of the measures being taken to embed some of the government's reforms in the legal framework. He said the objective was to ensure that policies and institutional changes were not left entirely to the discretion of successive governments.

title: JUSAG declares indefinite nationwide strike from November 2
snippet: Accra, Oct. 30, GNA – The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has declared an indefinite nationwide strike, effective Monday, November 2, 2026, over what it said…
content: Accra, Oct. 30, GNA – The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) has declared an indefinite nationwide strike, effective Monday, November 2, 2026, over what it said is the Government’s failure to approve and pay reviewed salaries and allowances for its members. Mr Abdulai Yakubu, General Secretary of JUSAG, announced the decision at a press conference held at the Supreme Court on Friday. He directed all Judicial Service staff not to report for work until the President approved the reviewed salaries and paid them in November, together with arrears covering January to October 2026. “All staff of the Judicial Service are directed not to report for work from Monday, November 2, 2026, unless and until His Excellency the President complies with Article 149 and CI 141 by approving our new salaries and paying them in November 2026, together with all arrears from January to October 2026,” he said. Mr Yakubu said security staff were to remain at their posts to safeguard the Service’s properties during the strike. He also instructed drivers to hand over official vehicles in their custody to the Transport Department, adding that no driver should operate an official vehicle or drive any officer or judge for the duration of the strike. Mr Yakubu further directed that no registrar should open or be compelled to open any registry or court for official business during the industrial action. He urged staff who were pressured or threatened by Management to report to work or perform official duties during the strike to decline and immediately report such incidents to JUSAG. “The Association would respond collectively and through lawful means to any attempt to intimidate or coerce its members,” he said. Mr Yakubu recalled that JUSAG notified the National Labour Commission (NLC) on October 23, of its intention to embark on an indefinite strike “following the Government’s failure to approve the Judicial Council’s recommendations on the review of salaries of Judicial Service employees.” He said the notification outlined efforts made since December 2025 to secure a salary review for 2026, but those efforts had yielded no results. He said growing frustration among members had prompted the National Executive Council (NEC) to demand approval of the Judicial Council’s recommendations by October 30, 2026, and payment of the reviewed salaries in November, together with the outstanding arrears. Mr Yakubu said the NEC had resolved that failure to meet the demands by November 1 would result in an indefinite strike from November 2. He said the notification to the NLC was copied to the Ministers of Jobs, Labour and Employment, and Finance; the Attorney-General and Minister of Justice; the Executive Secretary to the President; and the Judicial Secretary. He said the stakeholders were, therefore, fully aware of the Association’s concerns. However, he criticised the Ministry responsible for employment for failing to act until October 26, when the NLC directed it to convene a meeting of the parties to resolve the matter and report back. Mr Yakubu said the NLC had scheduled the parties to report back on November 6, four days after the strike was due to begin. He also said the Ministry of Jobs, Labour and Employment had scheduled a meeting for November 3, after the commencement of the strike. Mr Yakubu further criticised a proposal by the Ministry of Finance to pay the outstanding arrears in three instalments without specifying a payment timeline. He said the proposal was made without consultation with JUSAG, which he described as the principal party representing the affected beneficiaries. He said the Government’s handling of the matter had left the Association disappointed, adding that members had exercised patience and made several efforts to secure their legitimate entitlements. “We have been patient, we have been reasonable, we have gone the extra mile, and our patience has been taken for granted,” he said. GNA Edited by Agnes Boye-Doe Reporter: Joyce Danso joyce.danso@gna.org.gh

title: Director-General CID engages regional police officers to strengthen crime investigation
snippet: By Samuel Ackon Assin Fosu (C/R), Oct. 30, GNA – The Criminal Investigations Department (CID) has begun a series of engagements with police officers across the regions to…
content: By Samuel Ackon Assin Fosu (C/R), Oct. 30, GNA – The Criminal Investigations Department (CID) has begun a series of engagements with police officers across the regions to assess their performance, address operational challenges and introduce new investigative technologies to strengthen crime-fighting efforts. Commissioner of Police (COP) Lydia Yaako Donkor, Director-General of the CID, disclosed this during a visit to the Central North Police Region, following an earlier engagement with officers of the Central East Police Region at Kasoa. COP Donkor said the engagements were focused particularly on detectives, with the aim of reviewing achievements in crime investigations, encouraging improved performance and introducing officers to new technologies acquired by the CID. She also emphasised the importance of intelligence gathering, digital forensics and international cooperation in identifying, investigating and prosecuting criminal offenders. According to the CID Director-General, the regional visits formed part of an ongoing effort to strengthen police investigations, build the capacity of officers and improve crime-fighting operations across the country. Responding to concerns about transportation challenges facing the cybercrime unit in the Central North Police Region, COP Donkor said the CID was considering measures to strengthen collaboration between its headquarters and regional cybercrime units. She explained that the proposed system would assign specific regions to investigators at the CID headquarters to facilitate the efficient handling of cybercrime cases from those areas. COP Donkor noted that while the CID headquarters continued to handle a large number of cybercrime cases, regional units were also confronted with similar challenges that required coordinated support. She said concerns raised by officers during the engagement had reinforced the need to implement the proposed arrangement to bridge operational gaps and enhance service delivery. The Director-General commended the Central North Regional Police Commander and personnel of the command for their dedication, professionalism and commitment to duty. She acknowledged that police officers continued to face operational challenges but assured them that management would address their concerns as resources and opportunities became available. COP Donkor urged personnel to remain committed to the vision of the Ghana Police Service and support the efforts of the Inspector-General of Police to improve policing and public safety nationwide. She also appealed to the public to engage police commanders directly and report grievances through established channels rather than resorting immediately to the media. According to her, effective collaboration between the police and the public remained essential for addressing security concerns and promoting national development. GNA Edited by Alice Tettey /Lydia Kukua Asamoah 30 October 2026 Reporter: Samuel Ackon

title: Curious Minds invests in youth jobs to break cycle of child labour
snippet: By Samuel Ackon Assin Nsueam (C/R), Oct. 30, GNA – Curious Minds Ghana (CMG), in partnership with UNICEF Ghana and other development partners, has launched a youth empowerment…
content: By Samuel Ackon Assin Nsueam (C/R), Oct. 30, GNA – Curious Minds Ghana (CMG), in partnership with UNICEF Ghana and other development partners, has launched a youth empowerment project in the Assin South District of the Central Region to help address child labour through skills development and civic engagement. The project, dubbed “Empowering Young People Against Child Labour Through Civic Engagement and Skills Development,” seeks to equip young people with relevant skills and improve their access to learning, entrepreneurship and sustainable livelihood opportunities. A key component of the initiative is the Youth Agency Marketplace, a digital platform designed to connect young people to online courses, mentorship opportunities, volunteer programmes, entrepreneurship support and employment opportunities. The programme targets young people between the ages of 15 and 35 and encourages them to acquire marketable skills, participate in community development activities and take advantage of opportunities that can enhance their livelihoods. Speaking to the media after the launch, Mr Samuel Quaye, Programmes Manager of Curious Minds Ghana, said empowering young people with relevant skills and opportunities was critical to addressing some of the underlying vulnerabilities associated with child labour. He explained that the project was being implemented under the Child Labour Multisectoral and Multistakeholder Public-Private Partnership initiative in four districts across the country. The beneficiary districts are Assin South in the Central Region, Ayensuano in the Eastern region, Asunafo North in the Ahafo region, and Bibiani-Anhwiaso-Bekwai in the Western North region. Mr Quaye said the initiative sought to create sustainable pathways for young people to access education, employment and entrepreneurial opportunities, thereby reducing the economic pressures that often contribute to child labour. Meanwhile, Mr Jonathan Birikorang, District Chief Executive for Assin South, identified economic hardship, limited access to education and skills training, and inadequate livelihood opportunities as some of the major factors contributing to child labour. He assured stakeholders that the District Assembly was ready to collaborate with Curious Minds Ghana, UNICEF and other partners to intensify efforts aimed at combating child labour in the district. Mr Birikorang expressed confidence that the programme would empower young people, strengthen community participation and contribute to efforts to eliminate child labour while promoting sustainable development. GNA Edited by Alice Tettey/Lydi a Kukua Asamoah Reporter: Samuel Ackon

title: MIIF, Forestry Commission target planting 30,000 trees to restore Subri forest
snippet: By Mildred Siabi-Mensah Sekyere Krobo (W/R), Oct. 30, GNA – The Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF), in partnership with the Forestry Commission (FC), has launched a five-year forest…
content: By Mildred Siabi-Mensah Sekyere Krobo (W/R), Oct. 30, GNA – The Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF), in partnership with the Forestry Commission (FC), has launched a five-year forest reforestation programme aimed at planting 30,000 trees to restore 50 hectares of degraded land within the Subri River Forest Reserve in the Western Region. The initiative, undertaken as part of MIIF's Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) programme, seeks to restore the ecological integrity of the forest reserve, conserve biodiversity and promote the sustainable management of Ghana's natural resources. Mr Solomon Dawson, Head of Compliance and Enforcement at MIIF and Project Lead, said the programme demonstrated a shared commitment to restoring Ghana's natural environment, safeguarding its ecological heritage and promoting responsible management of the country's mineral wealth. He said mineral resource management must extend beyond financial returns and ESG disclosures to encompass environmental protection and the long-term well-being of communities. Mr Dawson explained that the sustainable management of Ghana's mineral resources required responsible stewardship of natural assets that support the economy, communities and future generations. According to him, that commitment had informed MIIF's ESG agenda, particularly its focus on biodiversity conservation and the responsible management of natural resources within the mining sector. “While mining contributes significantly to national development, its environmental and social implications demand deliberate, sustained and responsible interventions,” he said. Mr Dawson said MIIF partnered the Forestry Commission to identify practical measures to support environmental restoration and sustainable natural resource management within the 50-hectare project area at the Subri Forest Reserve. He stressed, however, that the success of the programme would depend on sustained maintenance, monitoring, protection and active community participation. “As a nation endowed with valuable resources, we must remain conscious that the benefits derived from our mineral wealth should not come at the expense of our forests, water bodies, biodiversity and the livelihoods of communities,” he said. Dr Sarfo Adu, Executive Director of the Forestry Commission, said an attempted invasion of parts of the Subri River Forest Reserve by armed illegal mining operators on October 17, 2026, underscored the challenges confronting the Commission in carrying out its constitutional mandate to protect and preserve the nation's forests. He reaffirmed the Commission's commitment to supporting the rehabilitation and restoration of degraded forest reserves across the country. Dr Adu expressed concern that illegal mining, farming and logging activities continued to destroy forest reserves, depriving the nation of critical environmental and economic benefits derived from forest resources. Mrs Justina Nelson, Chief Executive Officer of MIIF, said the initiative reflected the Fund's commitment to responsible mineral wealth management and environmental stewardship. She noted that while mineral resource extraction generated significant economic opportunities, such benefits must be balanced with the responsibility to protect the ecosystems that sustain communities. “We believe that responsible resource management must consider not only the value we generate today, but also the environmental legacy tomorrow,” she said. Mrs Nelson commended corporate institutions, the Sekyere Krobo community, traditional authorities and the District Assembly for their cooperation and support for the initiative. She urged stakeholders to take ownership of the project and help protect the restored areas to ensure the long-term success of the biodiversity conservation effort. Mr Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, Minister of Lands and Natural Resources, in a speech read on his behalf, reaffirmed the Ministry's support for the programme. He said the survival and growth of the planted trees would serve as a measure of the collective commitment to preserving the country's natural heritage. Nana Kwaw Badu II, Chief of Sekyere Krobo, expressed concern about the activities of chainsaw operators and illegal miners, which he said continued to undermine efforts to restore and protect the forest reserve. He appealed for incentives to be provided to farmers to encourage them to protect and nurture the planted trees to maturity. GNA Edited by Justina Hilda Paaga/Lydia Kukua Asamoah Reporter: Mildred Siabi-Mensah Mildred.siabi-mensah@gna.org.gh

title: TUTAG cautiously suspends ongoing industrial strike action
snippet: By Maxwell Awumah Ho, Oct 30, GNA-The National Congress of Technical University Teachers Association of Ghana (TUTAG), the highest decision-making body of the Association, after careful deliberations have…
content: By Maxwell Awumah Ho, Oct 30, GNA-The National Congress of Technical University Teachers Association of Ghana (TUTAG), the highest decision-making body of the Association, after careful deliberations have resolved to cautiously suspend the ongoing industrial strike action with immediate effect. This follows the constructive engagements between TUTAG, the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) on the orders of the Ministry of Education, and the Vice-Chancellors of Technical Universities, Ghana (VCTU-G), held on Wednesday. Professor Deodat E. Adenutsi, the National President of TUTAG, in a press engagement on Friday emphasised that the Association has cautiously suspended the strike; it has neither terminated nor called off the strike. “We wish to make this distinction clear to our members, students, management of the 10 technical universities, government and the general public. The decision to suspend the strike demonstrates TUTAG's trust and respect for VCTU-G, and restoring uninterrupted academic activities across the 10 technical universities,” he added. He said their collective decision was based on good faith and confidence in the negotiated process, with the expectation that the parties will translate the commitments made into concrete and verifiable actions. Key commitments and agreed resolutions were the outstanding remuneration of post-retirement contract staff with GTEC facilitating a meeting involving the relevant parties, including the Minister of Finance and VCTU-G, to resolve the outstanding remuneration of affected colleagues, not later than 14th November as well as implementation of the amended scheme of service: GTEC has agreed to grant a concession exempting affected categories. Again, classification of University Librarians as Academic Staff for which parties agreed a submission of a technical paper for consideration and implementation towards resolving the outstanding classification concerns in addition to continued dialogue and collaboration. All parties reaffirmed their commitment to sustained engagement and collaboration in the interest of industrial harmony and uninterrupted teaching and learning in technical universities. The TUTAG has therefore assured students, parents, guardians and the general public that academic life shall be fully restored across all technical university campuses with effect from Monday, 2nd November 2026, with all students expected to report to their respective universities for lectures and other scheduled academic activities on the said date. TUTAG entreats management of the various technical universities to put appropriate administrative measures in place to ensure that no student is disadvantaged or discriminated against as a consequence of this industrial action with special attention to newly admitted students who, owing to the strike, could not report to their respective campuses at the originally scheduled time. Prof Adenutsi reiterated the strike has been cautiously suspended, not terminated or called off; academic activities shall resume fully on Monday, 2nd November. “Our legitimate grievances remain outstanding until satisfactorily resolved, demands remain, our vigilance continues, and we are resolute in our commitment to finding a lasting solution to our concerns,” he said. The Association also appeals to its cherished members to remain united, disciplined and committed to the collective interests of all members adding TUTAG still believes that dialogue, mutual respect, institutional responsibility and good faith offer the most sustainable pathway to industrial harmony. GNA Edited by Benjamin Mensah Reported by: Maxwell Awumah Email address: Maxwell.awumah@gna.org.gh

title: GTA calls for responsible animal welfare practices in tourism sector
snippet: By Mildred Siabi-Mensah Takoradi, Oct. 30, GNA – The Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) has called on tourism and hospitality operators to adopt responsible animal welfare practices to enhance…
content: By Mildred Siabi-Mensah Takoradi, Oct. 30, GNA – The Ghana Tourism Authority (GTA) has called on tourism and hospitality operators to adopt responsible animal welfare practices to enhance Ghana's reputation as an ethical, safe and sustainable tourist destination. Mr Henry Yeleduor, Western Regional Director of the GTA, said the treatment of animals in hotels, restaurants, tourist attractions and tour operations increasingly influenced visitors' perceptions of destinations. He said animal welfare was not only a matter of compassion but also a key component of service standards, quality assurance and responsible tourism. Mr Yeleduor made the call during an animal welfare stakeholder engagement organised by the GTA in collaboration with the Animal Welfare League in Takoradi. The engagement was held on the theme: "Promoting Responsible Animal Welfare Practices in Ghana's Tourism and Hospitality Sector." He noted that as tourism continued to grow, operators needed to pay closer attention to global expectations regarding ethical and sustainable tourism practices. Mr Yeleduor said international visitors, cruise tourists and domestic travellers were increasingly concerned about the safety, ethical treatment and welfare of animals at tourism destinations. He observed that the expected arrival of cruise passengers aboard the Silver Muse on October 31 further underscored the need for tourism operators to uphold responsible animal welfare standards. According to him, the draft Animal Welfare Policy provides a proposed framework to guide the treatment and management of animals within the tourism and hospitality industry. The framework seeks to ensure the provision of adequate food and water, suitable shelter and living conditions, protection from pain and distress, and opportunities for animals to express natural behaviours. It also emphasises staff awareness, veterinary care, responsible sourcing of animals and the proper management of interactions between animals and visitors. Mr Yeleduor said the engagement sought to familiarise stakeholders with the principles of animal welfare under Ghanaian laws and international best practices, while highlighting how poor treatment of animals could negatively affect destination image and visitor satisfaction. He added that the programme was expected to help participants identify practical measures to improve animal welfare standards in hotels, restaurants, tour operations and tourist attractions. Mr Yeleduor urged participants to contribute their experiences and practical ideas to the discussions and become advocates for responsible animal welfare practices in the Western region and across the country. He reaffirmed the GTA's commitment to collaborating with the Animal Welfare League and other industry stakeholders to promote practices that protect animals while enhancing visitors' experiences. Mr Yeleduor thanked facilitators, partners and participants for supporting the initiative and expressed optimism that the deliberations would yield practical outcomes for the tourism and hospitality sector. GNA Edited by Justina Hilda Paaga/ Lydia Kukua Asamoah Reporter: Mildred Siabi-Mensah Mildred.siabi-mensah@gna.org.gh

title: JUSAG Declares Indefinite Strike From Monday Over Salary Review
snippet: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana, JUSAG, has declared an indefinite strike effective Monday, November 2, 2026, over government's failure to approve and implement reviewed salaries for staff of the Judicial Service. The declaration was made on Friday, October 30, 2026, after the deadline set by the union elapsed without results. The union has […]
content: The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana, JUSAG, has declared an indefinite strike effective Monday, November 2, 2026, over government's failure to approve and implement reviewed salaries for staff of the Judicial Service. The declaration was made on Friday, October 30, 2026, after the deadline set by the union elapsed without results. The union has advised court users, disputing parties and the general public to take note, as all Judicial Service staff are expected to stay away from work from Monday until their demands are met and leadership communicates otherwise. According to the declaration by the leadership, under Article 149 and C.I. 141, salaries and conditions of service of Judicial Service staff are determined by the President on the advice of the Judicial Council, with Regulation 25 providing for annual review. In line with this, the union said it submitted a proposal to the Judicial Council in December 2025 to aid its advice to the President. Following delays, a reminder was sent and the Judicial Council subsequently concluded its work and submitted its advice to the Presidency. Approval from the Presidency however delayed, prompting another reminder from the union warning that further delay could jeopardize industrial harmony. The leadership said appeals were made at several fora, including the 2nd Quadrennial Delegates Conference in Tamale where the Chief of Staff assured that the message would be taken to the Presidency, a Chief Justice staff durbar at the Tema High Court, and the recently ended MJG conference at Labadi Beach, but no positive results were achieved. Growing frustration among staff led the National Executive Council to hold an emergency meeting where it resolved to demand approval of the Judicial Council's advice on salaries by 30th October 2026 and payment of the approved salary in November 2026 together with arrears from January to October 2026, failing which an indefinite strike would commence on Monday, November 2. As a law-abiding union, JUSAG said it notified the National Labour Commission on Friday, 23rd October 2026 of its intention to strike, with notifications also sent to the Minister for Jobs, Labour Relations and Employment, Minister for Finance, Attorney General, Executive Secretary to the Office of the President, and the Judicial Secretary. The union expressed dissatisfaction with the handling of the matter, saying the Minister waited until last Monday when directed by the NLC to convene a meeting and that the NLC was expecting a report by November 3, 2026, when its deadline to government was October 30, which showed lack of commitment. The Ministry later invited the association to a meeting on Tuesday, November 3, a date after the strike takes effect. The union said the invitation did not include the Office of the President, which has the constitutional authority to approve the salaries, and included parties who ought not to be part of the discussion. It also said it chanced upon a letter from the Ministry of Finance which attempted to address the demands but was prepared without its input. Declaring the strike, the leadership stated that owing to the failure on the part of government to meet the demands and with today being the last day given to government, and it being past 4 PM without the demands being met, in compliance with the decision of its NEC, it hereby declares an indefinite strike starting from Monday, November 2, 2026. By this declaration, all staff of the Judicial Service are expected to stay home from Monday until the demands are met. The union advised persons who have cases on Monday not to show up at the courts, as staff will not be available. title: GOLD Fields Pumps $4.26bn In Ghanaian Businesses
snippet: Gold Fields Ghana Limited has invested US$4.26 billion in local businesses over the past five years, with US$2.59 billion going to businesses in its host communities, as the mining company intensifies efforts to strengthen local enterprise development. The company said it had consistently maintained an in-country procurement spend of 93 per cent over the period, […]
content: Gold Fields Ghana Limited has invested US$4.26 billion in local businesses over the past five years, with US$2.59 billion going to businesses in its host communities, as the mining company intensifies efforts to strengthen local enterprise development. The company said it had consistently maintained an in-country procurement spend of 93 per cent over the period, underscoring its commitment to ensuring that more economic benefits from its mining operations remained within Ghana. Speaking at the third Gold Fields Suppliers Conference at the Akoon Clubhouse at its Tarkwa Mine on October 28 and 29, 2026 the company’s Senior Vice-President and Managing Director, Mr Elliot Twum, said local procurement expenditure reached GH¢4.7 billion between January and June 2026.Of that amount, GH¢4.2 billion went to 124 suppliers in its host communities. The conference, held under the theme, “Partnership for Enduring Value: Building Resilient Supply Chain Beyond Mining,” brought together more than 300 local and international suppliers to discuss business partnerships and opportunities for sustainable growth. Mr Twum whose speech was read on his behalf said Gold Fields’ commitment to local content went beyond regulatory compliance, stressing the importance of developing strong Ghanaian enterprises capable of contributing to the wider economy. “Our commitment to local content, however, isn’t just about compliance,” he said, adding that the company’s engagement with Ghanaian-owned businesses predated the Minerals and Mining (Local Content and Local Participation) Regulations, 2020, also known as L.I. 2431. He cited Zen Petroleum, GASO, Genser and Western Transport Services as examples of local businesses that had contributed to the company’s operations and grown through sustained partnerships. He, however, cautioned suppliers to maintain high standards of quality, safety, environmental responsibility and corporate governance to meet the operational and sustainability requirements of the mining industry. Mr Twum also disclosed that more than GH¢53 million had been channelled into socioeconomic development through the Gold Fields Ghana Foundation so far this year. Among the projects was an alternative road linking New Atuabo to the Bogoso Junction Highway, constructed by Woodbine Limited, a local contractor from New Atuabo. The road had reduced travel time from 30 minutes to 10 minutes. He said 150 young people from the company’s host communities had received scholarships this year. Since the Foundation was established 20 years ago, more than 3,000 students had received full support for tertiary education. Employment from host communities had reached 70 per cent, while the company had contributed more than GH¢3.5 billion to the Government of Ghana as of October 2026, he added. For his part, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT), Professor Bernard Kumi-Boateng, urged suppliers to use their partnerships with mining companies to build resilient businesses capable of surviving beyond individual contracts and expanding into other sectors. Addressing the conference on the topic, “Partnerships with Lasting Legacies,” he said businesses that depended heavily on one mine, customer or contract risked collapse when operations changed or the relationship ended. “Enduring value is what a partnership leaves behind that can stand on its own. It is not the cheque,” he said. He encouraged suppliers to pursue opportunities in energy, construction, manufacturing, agriculture and infrastructure, while strengthening their business systems, obtaining professional certifications and training younger workers. He also urged businesses to diversify their customer base, recommending that no single customer should account for more than half of their revenue. Professor Kumi-Boateng further called on suppliers to separate personal and business finances, invest in employees, strengthen leadership structures and adopt digital tools to improve business operations. He said mining companies, academic institutions and suppliers needed to collaborate more closely to equip local enterprises with the skills and systems required to compete in other industries. The two-day conference forms part of Gold Fields Ghana’s engagement with its business partners to strengthen supply-chain relationships and promote sustainable economic opportunities beyond individual mining contracts.

title: Agongo targets self-employment with 10,000 sewing machine initiative
snippet: Businessman and philanthropist, Alhaji Seidu Agongo, has launched a nationwide drive to distribute 10,000 sewing machines to vulnerable women and young people, in an initiative aimed at turning practical skills into sustainable livelihoods. The programme, being implemented in partnership with the National Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme (NEIP), seeks to equip beneficiaries with the tools to […]
content: Businessman and philanthropist, Alhaji Seidu Agongo, has launched a nationwide drive to distribute 10,000 sewing machines to vulnerable women and young people, in an initiative aimed at turning practical skills into sustainable livelihoods. The programme, being implemented in partnership with the National Entrepreneurship and Innovation Programme (NEIP), seeks to equip beneficiaries with the tools to establish or expand tailoring and dressmaking businesses rather than depend solely on limited employment opportunities. More than 800 sewing machines were distributed during the first phase of the initiative, with subsequent distributions expected to take place in phases across the country. Speaking after the presentation of the first batch on Wednesday, Mr Agongo urged beneficiaries to take advantage of the opportunity, stressing that talent alone was insufficient without discipline, commitment and hard work. "You should not be shy about your talents. Once it is a genuine talent, pursue it and commit your energy, your heart and your time to them,” he said. He added that success was achievable for people from humble backgrounds if they remained focused and worked consistently towards their goals. “Breakthroughs are not miracles you only see in movies or read about in books. They are real, but they must be backed by hard work, commitment and a goal,” he said. From skills to livelihoods Mr Agongo said many young Ghanaians possessed the creativity and abilities needed to succeed, but lacked the resources and opportunities to translate them into productive ventures. He explained that the sewing machine initiative was intended to bridge that gap by providing practical equipment to people who could use their skills to generate income and become economically independent. The initiative also reflects a broader focus on entrepreneurship and vocational skills as pathways to employment, particularly for women and young people seeking to establish businesses with relatively modest resources. Interested applicants are required to complete a form available on Mr Agongo’s social media platforms to be considered for a free sewing machine. The founder of the now-collapsed Heritage Bank Limited said the programme was part of his longstanding commitment to sharing opportunities and supporting vulnerable members of society. "We all need kindness. Whatever your situation, I will say don't despair. I want to help everyone as much as possible. I want to live by people's happiness,” he said adding “there is room for everyone if we genuinely support each other. I have always believed in sharing, supporting and being there for everyone whenever I can.” He expressed the hope that beneficiaries would use the opportunity to improve their circumstances and extend similar support to people around them. title: Beyond Grammar: Are We Creating Classrooms Where Students Can Speak English Without Fear?
snippet: A student raises a hand to answer a question, pauses, and then lowers it. Another has an idea but struggles to find the right words. Somewhere in the classroom, a learner who attempts to speak English incorrectly becomes the subject of laughter. The next time an opportunity arises, that learner chooses silence. These moments may […]
content: A student raises a hand to answer a question, pauses, and then lowers it. Another has an idea but struggles to find the right words. Somewhere in the classroom, a learner who attempts to speak English incorrectly becomes the subject of laughter. The next time an opportunity arises, that learner chooses silence. These moments may appear insignificant, but they raise a serious question: are our classrooms helping students develop confidence in English, or are some learners gradually learning to remain silent? To explore students’ experiences, the authors gathered responses from selected students at Kumasi Girls’ Senior High School, Abrepo–Kumasi, through eight questions about learning the English language. Their responses revealed that the challenges extend beyond grammar, spelling and pronunciation. They also involve fear, confidence, teaching methods, access to learning materials and the attitudes students encounter when they make mistakes. The students’ responses send an important message to all education stakeholders, including teachers, school leaders, parents and policymakers: improving students’ confidence in English requires supportive learning environments in which mistakes are treated as opportunities for improvement rather than occasions for ridicule. The Struggle Behind the Silence One student attributed learners’ difficulties in speaking English to limited vocabulary, while another identified pronunciation difficulties and the fear of ridicule by classmates as major obstacles. These experiences reveal a problem that deserves closer attention. Students cannot develop their language skills through practice if they constantly fear the reactions of those listening to them. The fear of making a mistake can become a barrier to learning when the classroom fails to distinguish between correcting an error and humiliating the person who makes it. When English Becomes a Barrier Across Subjects The students also described how reading and understanding English affect their learning in other subjects. One learner explained that understanding English makes it easier to explain concepts in other subjects. These observations remind us that language proficiency is closely connected to students’ opportunities to demonstrate what they know. A learner may understand a scientific concept but struggle to interpret the question or express the answer clearly. What Students Say Needs to Change Many students recommended reading and spelling competitions to motivate students. Several called for lessons that are more practical, interactive and enjoyable. The students also emphasised the importance of teacher–student relationships. They wanted teachers to interact positively with them, use engaging teaching methods and avoid creating an atmosphere in which learners are afraid to participate. One response captured this concern particularly well: some teaching methods make students so frightened that they no longer want to learn the subject. That observation should challenge every educator. As language teachers, we must not allow fear to prevent our learners from expressing their opinions in class. The classroom environment should be warm and friendly. A demanding classroom can still be supportive, respectful and encouraging. Students, too, have responsibilities. They must read widely, practise speaking, research unfamiliar words, write regularly and learn to accept constructive correction. Confidence is not built overnight; it develops through repeated opportunities to practise. Turning Recommendations into Action The students' suggestions should not remain words on paper. Schools can begin with practical, affordable steps. First, English departments can establish reading clubs and organise regular spelling, vocabulary and public-speaking activities. Teachers should also establish clear expectations against ridicule. When a student mispronounces a word, the response should be correction and encouragement, not laughter. When a learner struggles to construct a sentence, the teacher can help the student rebuild it correctly. The Ghana Education Service, the Ministry of Education and school leaders should support literacy initiatives that combine effective language instruction with regular opportunities for reading, speaking and constructive feedback. Teacher development should also emphasise ways of correcting errors without discouraging learners from participating. The perspectives gathered from the students do not represent every learner in Ghana, but they provide useful insights that schools can explore further. Let Us Give Every Student a Voice The English language challenge cannot be addressed by asking students to speak confidently while ignoring the conditions that make them afraid to speak. Neither can it be solved by teaching grammar alone when learners also need vocabulary, reading opportunities, meaningful practice and encouragement. We must build classrooms where students can ask questions, attempt unfamiliar words, make mistakes and improve without being ridiculed. A learner's first attempt may be imperfect. The next may be better. With guidance, practice and encouragement, progress becomes possible. The question is not simply whether our students can speak English today. It is whether our schools are giving them the support, resources and confidence to speak it better tomorrow. Let us teach the language, nurture the confidence and protect the courage it takes to speak. When students are no longer afraid to use their voices, learning has a better chance to flourish. By Mr. Isaac Nyarko Antwi (English Tutor, GES; Mentor) and Ms. Michealla Koduah (Final-Year Student, UEW; Mentee) For more news , join The Chronicle Newspaper channel on WhatsApp: https://whatsapp.com/channel/0029VbBSs55E50UqNPvSOm2z

title: Editorial: Empire Cement Quit Notice Is Welcome News
snippet: The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) has directed Empire Cement Ghana Limited to submit a comprehensive plan to relocate its cement grinding and bagging facility away from the Densu Delta Ramsar Site. In a directive dated October 28, 2026 the EPA gave the company 30 days to present a relocation strategy including alternative industrial sites, implementation […]
content: The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) has directed Empire Cement Ghana Limited to submit a comprehensive plan to relocate its cement grinding and bagging facility away from the Densu Delta Ramsar Site. In a directive dated October 28, 2026 the EPA gave the company 30 days to present a relocation strategy including alternative industrial sites, implementation timelines, worker protection measures and operational transition arrangements. The Authority also reaffirmed that a Closure Notice issued on September 14, 2026 remains in force. The EPA said concerns about the facility dates back to June 2020, when it ordered the company to halt construction and identify an alternative location because of land-use incompatibility. Environmental assessments subsequently identified potential public health concerns, flood risks and the movement of heavy-duty vehicles through surrounding communities. Empire Cement must secure the necessary environmental and land-use approvals for its new location and work with relevant institutions to decommission the existing facility and rehabilitate the site. Unauthorised operations could attract sanctions under the Environmental Protection Act, 2025 (Act 1124). The EPA’s directive ordering Empire Cement Ghana Limited to submit a plan to relocate its cement grinding and bagging facility away from the Densu Delta Ramsar Site is welcome news. It is also long overdue. The EPA deserves commendation for taking this step to protect the environment and the health and safety of surrounding communities. However, the circumstances leading to this directive raise serious questions about how a facility of this nature was allowed to operate in such an environmentally sensitive location in the first place. A Ramsar site is internationally recognised for its importance as a wetland. Such areas support biodiversity, help regulate water flows and provide essential ecological services. The Densu Delta is no exception. Locating an industrial facility with the potential to generate dust and other forms of pollution close to such an important ecosystem should have attracted the strictest scrutiny from the outset. Indeed, according to the EPA, concerns about Empire Cement’s location date back to June 2020, when the Authority ordered the company to halt construction and find an alternative site because of land-use incompatibility. Subsequent assessments also identified potential public health concerns, flood risks and the movement of heavy-duty vehicles through surrounding communities. This raises a fundamental question: if these concerns were identified years ago, why has it taken this long to reach the present stage? The proximity of a cement facility to residential communities is itself a matter of concern. Cement grinding and bagging can generate dust, while the movement of heavy-duty vehicles can expose residents to additional risks. Without effective safeguards, these activities may compromise air quality, public health and residents’ quality of life. The potential consequences for the surrounding wetland make the situation even more troubling. The EPA’s directive, therefore, must not remain another regulatory announcement without meaningful enforcement. Empire Cement has 30 days to submit a comprehensive relocation plan, identify an alternative industrial site, outline implementation timelines and provide measures to protect workers during the transition. The Authority must ensure that these requirements are met and that the existing Closure Notice remains in force. The company should not be allowed to resume unauthorised operations while the notice is effective. Equally important is the proper decommissioning of the existing facility and rehabilitation of the affected site. Beyond this particular case, the government and environmental regulators must examine how industrial permits are granted and monitored. Sensitive wetlands and residential communities should not become places where industrial operators are permitted to establish facilities first, only for environmental and public health concerns to be addressed years later. There must also be accountability for decisions that allowed such a potentially incompatible land use to proceed despite the environmental sensitivities involved. The relocation directive is a step in the right direction. But protecting the Densu Delta requires more than a directive; it requires consistent enforcement, transparent oversight and a commitment to preventing similar mistakes. The EPA must see this process through to its logical conclusion. Environmental protection cannot be an afterthought. It must begin before the first block is laid. title: Marketing Communications Policy for the University of Ghana
snippet:
This University of Ghana Marketing Communications policy
guides the University of Ghana (UG) community in its marketing
communication activities recognising that all such activities
should be coordinated from a Marketing and Service Excellence
Unit located within the Office of Institutional Advancement.
The Marketing and Service Excellence Unit exercises oversight
responsibility for the co-ordination of all official internal and
external marketing communication activities of the entire
University. No marketing consultants, marketing research
firms, public relations agencies, brand design agencies, graphic
design firms, web design firms, independent design consultants
or social media consultants will be communicated with, without
the prior approval of the Marketing and Service Excellence Unit.
For the purpose of this policy, Marketing Communications
refers to advertising, direct marketing, branding, packaging,
online presence, printed materials, public relations activities,
sales presentations, sponsorships, trade show appearances and
all activities connected with the promotion of the University of
Ghana in local and international markets.

title: Cultural factors constraining the introduction of family planning among the kassena-nankana of northern Ghana
snippet: This study presents a focus group investigation of reasons why women in a rural, Sahelian community are reluctant to adopt family planning even when convenient services are made freely available. First, women opting to practice contraception must do so at considerable risk of social ostracism or familial conflict. Implementing individual preference is something that must be done without the support of others. Second, few women view personal decisions about contraceptives as theirs to make. Women and children are the property of the corporate family-kin and community militate against reproductive control. Third, although children are highly valued for a variety of economic, social, and cultural reasons, mortality risks remain extremely high. Low fertility imposes the unacceptable risk that a woman will have no surviving children at the end of her reproductive life. Taken together, these findings attest to the inadequacy of service strategies focused on the contribution of distribution, individual agency, or personal choice. Outreach should also build a sense of community legitimacy for the program, collective health action, and traditional leadership support for family planning behavior.

title: Factors Influencing the Performance of State-Owned Enterprises in Ghana: The Case of Electricity Company of Ghana and Ghana Buffer Stock Company Ltd
snippet:
State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) in Ghana have played a key role in national development, yet 
their performance has been inconsistent. Initially established to drive industrialization and 
provide essential services, many SOEs became financially unsustainable by the 1980s. Despite 
ongoing reforms to enhance governance and financial management, many SOEs still face low 
productivity, financial mismanagement, and weak governance. Additionally, governance 
reforms in Ghana, including performance contracts, have not been adequately assessed for 
effectiveness. To bridge these gaps, this study applies Agency Theory to analyze governance 
challenges and performance drivers in Ghanaian SOEs. The study sample 20 respondents from 
the Electricity Company of Ghana and Ghana Buffer Stock Company Ltd. From the data 
analysis the study revealed that looking at the historical analysis of the performance of the 
SOEs there is an improvement in the governance and management structures of the SOEs. 
There has also been technological adoption and modernization and a balanced social mandate 
with commercial viability among the SOEs. However, political interference and governance 
still remains as a key challenge to SOEs in Ghana. Further, in assessing the factors that affect 
the economic performance of the SOEs, the study revealed that regulation environment, 
financial management and market dynamics, human capital and operational efficiency, 
transparency, accountability, and anti-corruption measures were the key factors affecting the 
economic performance of SOEs in Ghana. Subsequently, looking at the regulatory frameworks 
in enhancing the governance performance of the SOEs, some of the participants of the study 
highlighted that role clarification and reduction of bureaucratic overlap, accountability and 
performance-based incentives, adaptability to technological and market changes, and need for 
continuous capacity building are some of the regulatory frameworks that would help enhance 
the governance performance of the SOEs in Ghana. Based on these findings the study was able 
to make some recommendations that will help improve the general performance of SOEs in 
Ghana.

title: Examining the Determinants of Employee Fraud and the Effectiveness in Managing Employee Fraud in the Banking
snippet: The general objective of this research was to examine the determinants of employee fraud in the banking sector of Ghana, using some selected universal banks as the case study. These objectives included ascertaining factors that drive employee fraud among universal banks in Ghana, examining the effectiveness of managing employee fraud among the universal banks in Ghana and identifying the challenges confronting the universal banks in the management of employee fraud in Ghana. The study was limited to selected local and foreign banks in Ghana. They included the GCB Bank, the Consolidated Bank Ghana, Ecobank Ghana Limited, and Access Bank Ghana Limited. The study targeted bank staff within the Greater Accra region of Ghana, comprising of both management and non-management staff. The research analysed the previous related studies by focusing on the theoretical reflections of the problem under investigation, examining the conceptual framework, and reviewing the extant empirical literatures with regards to the determinants of employee fraud in the banking sector of Ghana. The literature review revealed four factors that drive employee fraud in the banking sector, the four factors include opportunity, rationalization, pressure and capitalization. The respondents indicated that, all the four factors were key determinants of employee fraud in the banking sector of Ghana (M=3.58, SD=0.79). They all agreed that opportunity, rationalization, pressure, and capability were the key factors driving employee fraud in the banking sector of Ghana. The overall significance level of 0.3% further indicated that majority of the respondents agreed to all the issues raised with regards to the factors that were likely to drive employee fraud within the banking sector of Ghana. The research recommends that, structures must be put in place in order to reduce staff involvement in the fraud practices in the banking sector of Ghana and these structures include

title: Prophetess Laura Adorkor Kofi And The Back To Africa Mission: A Ghanaian Perspective
snippet:
This diesis is a contribution to the discourse on Laura Adorkor Kofi and her hack-to-Africa vision, The thesis engages in textual analysis of studies that have been done on Laura Kuti and explores grey areas covering her identity and Ghanaian citizenship. It engages in a comparative analysis of the various methodologies adopted by scholars who have studied Laura Kofi, and makes a case for the importance of oral narratives in accessing information about Laura Adorkor Kofi’s Ghanaian ancestry. The thesis is in two parts: The first part studies Laura Kofi from die United States of America perspective, while die second part studies Laura Kofi from the Ghanaian perspective. The first part analyses studies that have been done focusing on Kofi’s association with the Universal Negro Improvement Association (henceforth UNIA), her expulsion from the UNIA, her formation of the African Universal Church {henceforth AUG), her Patt-African and religious engagements and events leading to her demise. This part also discusses the difficulties she encountered and the successes she achieved within the period. The second part of the study* which focuses on her Ghanaian ancestry, analyses issues relating to her origin and attempts to solve the mystery surrounding her identity. This part explains why she is referred to as a Ghanaian, a princess and a prophetess, and why she bears the name Adorkor Kofi. The study explains the seeming contradictions in some of the existing literature and documents oral accounts from a descendant and other career of handed-down oral narrations of the
story of Laura Adorkor Kofi.

title: Environmental care in Ghana: A moral duty for Ghanaian Christians
snippet: Since human beings depend on the natural environment for survival, humans have the moral duty to ensure the sustainable use of the environment. Being part of the human family, Ghanaians have a share in this universal moral duty that involves the particular moral obligation to care for the natural environment within and outside the geographical area of the nation. Similarly, Christians are bound to observe God`s injunction to love their neighbour and care for creation. These notwithstanding, in Ghana, the natural environment is at the mercy of different forms of environmental abuses, thereby undermining the healthy survival of both the present and future generations. This paper challenges Ghanaian Christians to realize and accept that they have a moral duty to care for the environment and also recognize the urgent need to collaborate with the government, and other stakeholders to salvage the environmental crisis in Ghana

title: Multinational Telecommunication Companies and the International Relations of Ghana
snippet: International business has become possible because of globalisation which is the greater interdependence and interconnectedness that exist among countries and their citizens. Multinational Companies have been observed as one of the platforms to foster international relations between their countries of origin and the host country. This current study investigates the extent to which the activities of MTN and Vodafone which originate from South Africa and the United Kingdom respectively help to foster international relations between Ghana-South Africa and Ghana-United Kingdom. The study was situated within Realism theoretical framework specifically Neoclassical strand of Realism by Waltz, 1979. Using the mixed method research design for data collection and analysis, thematic analysis was used to analyse qualitative data. Quantitative data were examined using descriptive and inferential statistics. The study observes that the activities of MTN and Vodafone enhance Ghana-South Africa and Ghana-United Kingdom relations respectively. The study also observes that, MTN and Vodafone have contributed to the human resource development of the Ghanaian staff. The study recommends that, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration could consider partnering with the National Communication Authority for the benefit of synergy, and come up with policies that will enhance the international collaborations between Ghana and the countries of origin of the mobile telecommunication network companies. Also, Ghana telecommunication regulations and foreign policy could be prepared with inputs from the telecommunication companies concerned.

title: The origins, implementation and effects of Ghana's 1969 Aliens compliance order
snippet: This study situates the November 18, 1969 Aliens Compliance Order in a historical perspective and, with the employment of the internal-external approach, examines the context in which the expulsion order was enforced. Relying on both primary and secondary sources, the study reveals that various factors combined to make Ghana one of the preferred migrants’ destinations in West Africa, especially from the beginning of the nineteenth century to the 1960s. In the face of the growing immigrant population, the colonial, Nkrumah and NLC administrations all introduced immigration measures to control the influx of immigrants into Ghana. However, the colonial government and Nkrumah administration did not strictly enforce those regulations. The NLC attempted to remedy the situation, but it could not achieve much. When the Busia government was inaugurated, it immediately issued the expulsion order which caused the deportation of many immigrants in a manner never before attempted. The study demonstrates how the interplay of factors, such as the government’s desire to reduce the rate of unemployment and remittances from Ghana, combat crime, guarantee the security of the country, compel immigrants to comply with the immigration laws of Ghana, control the growth of the country’s population, ensure cultural homogeneity, clear the streets of immigrant destitutes and beggars, continue the policies of the NLC, and xenophobia on the part of some Ghanaians, at least to some extent, influenced the government’s decision to issue the expulsion order. iv The study observes that the decision was strictly enforced. Some of the immigrants who made efforts to secure permits were successful, but many were those who failed and, thus, had to leave Ghana, sometimes hastily. The study again shows that in some cases, the police and some ordinary citizens went to the extreme so that many of the expellees suffered in many ways, including loss of property and even death. The work indicates the economic, social and political repercussions of the expulsion on Ghana and the country’s foreign relations. In the end, the government did not fully realise the objectives for which it issued the Order, but some modest gains were made. The study finally appreciates the good intentions of the government in acting in the interest of Ghana, as was alleged, but frowns on the harsh manner in which the implementation was done. The study contends that if the government had been more cautious in executing the decision, it could have realised its objectives.

title: An Overview of Political and Economic Development in Ghana from 1957-2008
snippet:
This paper examines the overview of the political and economic development in Ghana from 1957 to the year
2008. The past five decade has witnessed morass in the political and the economic landscape of Ghana.
Governments, both civilian and military all came to power with the promise of a better Ghana for Ghanaians.
However, for over fifty years after independence, the country has not experienced a major economic take-off,
even though there has been some level of stability in the political terrain. The study adopted both primary and
secondary sources of data to examine the political and the economic development of Ghana from 1957 to 2008.
Out of 68 respondents, 52% asserted that Ghana, like most developing countries, lacks the capital needed to
enhance economic growth and development. Hence, donor assistance has played a significant role in the
development of the country.As a result of the continuous flow of assistance from the developed world to aid the
development of the country, Ghana has become aid dependent.Seventy two percent (72%) of Ghanaians are of
the view that Ghana is donor dependent. The inability of the country to internally generate revenue for budget
funding makes it impossible for the country to wean itself off donor assistance. This study therefore concludes
that political stability is very relevant in the search for sustainable economic growth and development in the
search for sustainable economic growth and development in Ghana

title: Role of higher education and science, technology and innovation in capacity development in Ghana
snippet: Ghana has shown keen interest in promoting Science, Technology and Innovation (STI), and Higher Education (HE). However, the STI and HE systems do not seem to be adequately focused on Ghana’s socio-economic needs.  Furthermore, existing STI and HE policies and programmes do not appear to be motivating enough to drive investments and technological upgrading. Consequently, many of the country’s important STI institutions are unable to effectively carry out their mandates. The study was undertaken to examine the role of STI and HE policies in capacity development in Ghana. The desk study showed that there has been a lot of investment in setting up STI and HE institutions which have yielded some positive outcomes especially in the country’s recent research output. Progress on Ghana’s capacity for STI looks encouraging, given that Ghana’s overall Africa Capacity Index is Medium primarily because of a narrow financing base. The country also currently has a comprehensive STI policy draft to work with up to 2024. However, there is the need for Ghana to put in place workable monitoring and evaluation strategies on STI and HE policies and programmes. This will enhance the impact of STI and HE on the economy of the country

title: Travel Motivations, Satisfaction Levels and Loyalty Intentions of International Tourists in Ghana
snippet:
To be successful in today’s competitive tourism marketplace, tourism marketers and hospitality managers need a deeper understanding of tourists’ behaviour. This study seeks to establish how more foreign tourists can be attracted to Ghana. This thesis investigated travel motivations, satisfaction levels and loyalty intentions of visitors to Ghana between 1st October 2009 and 1st May 2010. The mixed method research approach was adopted for the study. Accra, Kumasi and Cape Coast were chosen as the study areas. Accordingly, questionnaires were used to collect data from 405 tourists and in-depth interviews were granted to 100 tourists and 10 tourism marketers/managers. Factor analysis, Chi-square and the Pearson’s correlation techniques were used to analyse the data. Summations, tables, pictures and diagrams were used to present the results.
The study found that visitors’ main push motives (intrinsic desires) were the drive to escape, relaxation and the quest for knowledge while the pull motives (destination attractiveness) were the natural attractions, rich culture of the people, and cleanliness of the destination. A majority of the tourists were highly satisfied with their experiences and were prepared to revisit and recommend Ghana to others. However, the respondents disclosed a few concerns based on which innovative marketing strategies to adopt were suggested. Finally, based on the push-pull framework (Crompton, 1979), a modified behavioural model (the Travel Motivation, Satisfaction and Loyalty Model) was proposed to better explain tourists’ decision-making process and contribute to existing knowledge and practice on tourists’ behaviour.

title: Homosexuality and the youth in the catholic church: A case study in the Ejisu municipality
snippet:
ABSTRACT
Homosexuality is gradually becoming a controversial issue in Ghana today. Homosexuals are 
demanding to be given equal rights and treatment as heterosexuals in the Ghanaian society. Human 
rights organisations are claiming that all laws that discriminate against people on the basis of their 
sexual orientation, violates human rights. However, many nations globally, including Ghana, still 
maintain laws that discriminate against homosexual acts. In Ghana today, homosexuality is an illegal 
and ethical subject is attracting diverse opinions. Whilst some Western countries recognize 
homosexuality as legal and provide free movement as well as resident permits for same-sex couples, 
homosexuality is repressed, criminalized and forbidden in Ghana. A bill to criminate homosexuality 
in Ghana is before the Ghanaian Parliament for consideration. However, there has been an intense 
debate among Ghanaians on whether to legalize homosexuality or not. Homosexuality is common 
among the youth especially in boarding schools. Meanwhile most of them are Christians with some 
belonging to the Roman Catholic Church. As already mentioned, homosexual acts are illegal in 
Ghana for now, hence their acts are hidden and it is a problem to deal with especially, among the 
youth as peer pressure plays very important role in their decision making. This study aims at 
exploring the attitude of the youth in the Roman Catholic Church in the Ejisu Juaben Municipality 
towards homosexuality. A qualitative study is employed to investigate why the youth, engage in 
homosexuality, the Church’s pastoral role towards the youth in the Church concerning 
homosexuality and also to assess the views of the youth on the effects of homosexuality. The study 
further contributes to the current debate on homosexuality from the reactions of the Ghanaian youth 
in particular in relation to the global dimension.
